chapters.n: Ezekiel opens with a date and a place: he is among the Jewish exiles in Babylon, beside the Chebar canal, when the heavens open to him. The “thirtieth year” is probably his own age—the age when priests began serving.

f.g: Likely Ezekiel’s age; priests began full service at thirty.
A large irrigation canal near the city of Nippur in Babylonia.

chapters.n: The fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s exile dates the vision to about 593 BC. Jehoiachin and many leaders—Ezekiel included—had been deported in 597 BC, about a decade before Jerusalem’s final fall.

f.g: Also called Jeconiah or Coniah; king of Judah for three months before surrendering to Nebuchadnezzar.

chapters.n: Ezekiel is a priest, son of Buzi. Though far from the temple, he receives God’s word in a pagan land—a powerful message that the Lord is not confined to Jerusalem. “The hand of the LORD” signals prophetic power resting on him.

f.g: Another name for the Babylonians, from the ruling dynasty’s homeland in southern Mesopotamia.

f.w: the hand of the LORD was there upon him

chapters.n: Ezekiel sees a storm sweeping in from the north: a huge cloud, flashing fire, and a glowing radiance at its center. Storm, cloud, and fire are classic signs of God’s presence, as at Sinai.

f.g: A stormy wind.

f.w: a great cloud, and a fire

f.g: Hebrew ḥashmal—a gleaming substance, perhaps electrum (a gold-silver alloy). Its exact meaning is uncertain.

chapters.n: Out of the fire appear four living creatures with an overall human shape. Chapter 10 identifies them as cherubim, heavenly beings who attend God’s throne.
Each creature has four faces and four wings—able to face every direction at once, fitting servants of a God who sees everything.

f.g: Isaiah’s seraphim had six wings.

chapters.n: Their legs are straight, their feet like a calf’s hoof, and they gleam like polished bronze—images of strength, steadiness, and brilliance.

f.g: Polished bronze.

chapters.n: Under their wings they have human hands. Later one creature uses its hands to pass burning coals (10:7–8).
Their wings touch one another, and they move straight ahead without turning, since with faces on every side they never need to turn around.

f.w: they turned not when they went
f.g: They could move in any direction without turning.

chapters.n: The four faces—human, lion, ox, and eagle—are often understood as representing the best of creation: humanity, wild animals, domestic animals, and birds. Early Christians linked them with the four Gospel writers.

f.w: the face of a man, and the face of a lion

chapters.n: Two of each creature’s wings stretch upward to touch its neighbors, and two cover its body—an act of reverence before God.
The creatures move wherever “the spirit” directs them, in perfect obedience and unity.

f.w: whither the spirit was to go, they went
f.g: The Hebrew ruaḥ can mean spirit, wind, or will.

chapters.n: The creatures glow like burning coals and torches, with fire darting among them and lightning flashing out—an overwhelming display of holy power.
They dart back and forth like flashes of lightning—swift and dazzling.

f.w: as the appearance of a flash of lightning

chapters.n: Next Ezekiel notices a wheel on the ground beside each creature. The vision is becoming a chariot-throne—God on the move.

f.g: Later Jewish mystics called this vision the merkavah, the “chariot.”

chapters.n: The wheels sparkle like a precious stone, and each seems to be a wheel within a wheel—perhaps two wheels set crosswise so they can roll in any direction.

f.g: Hebrew tarshish, a gleaming gemstone, perhaps topaz or chrysolite.

f.w: a wheel in the middle of a wheel
f.g: Likely intersecting wheels, allowing movement in all four directions.

chapters.n: The wheels can go in any of the four directions without turning, matching the creatures.

f.w: they turned not when they went
f.g: The phrase echoes v. 9 and v. 12, stressing perfect, direct obedience.

chapters.n: The wheels’ rims are towering and awe-inspiring, and covered with eyes—a picture of God’s all-seeing knowledge.

f.g: The rims of the wheels.

chapters.n: Wheels and creatures move together, whether rolling on the ground or rising into the air.
The spirit that moves the creatures also moves the wheels. The whole chariot acts as one under God’s direction.

f.w: the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels
f.g: The wheels share the creatures’ life and will.

chapters.n: A repetition for emphasis: when the creatures go, stand, or rise, the wheels do the same. God’s presence is mobile—able to come even to exiles in Babylon.
Above the creatures’ heads stretches a platform like dazzling crystal—a sky-like dome.

f.g: An expanse or platform, the same word used for the sky in Genesis.
Awe-inspiring ice or crystal.

chapters.n: Beneath the platform each creature spreads two wings toward its neighbors and covers its body with the other two.

f.g: A posture of reverence and modesty before God.

chapters.n: The sound of their wings is like roaring waters, like the voice of the Almighty, like the noise of an army camp—sound as overwhelming as the sight.

f.w: like the noise of great waters

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai, an ancient name of God.

chapters.n: When the creatures stop and lower their wings, a voice comes from above the platform.

f.g: The source of authority is above the creatures—God himself.

chapters.n: Above the platform is a throne of sapphire-blue stone, and on it a figure who looks like a man. Ezekiel speaks carefully—“the likeness,” “the appearance”—because he is describing God. Latter-day Saints see here a witness that God has a glorified form in whose image man was made.

f.g: Probably lapis lazuli, deep blue.

f.w: the likeness as the appearance of a man

chapters.n: The figure glows like gleaming metal surrounded by fire, from the waist up and the waist down—radiant glory too bright to describe exactly.

f.g: Waist, hips.

chapters.n: The brightness is like a rainbow in the clouds—a symbol of God’s covenant faithfulness. Ezekiel concludes: this was the likeness of the glory of the LORD. Overwhelmed, he falls on his face and hears a voice speaking.

f.w: the bow that is in the cloud

chapters.n: The Lord addresses Ezekiel as “son of man,” a title used over 90 times in this book. Here it stresses Ezekiel’s humble mortality before God’s glory. God tells him to stand up so they can speak.

f.g: Hebrew ben-adam: “human being, mortal.” In Ezekiel it marks the prophet’s lowliness; later it becomes a title of Christ.

chapters.n: The Spirit enters Ezekiel and lifts him to his feet. He cannot even stand in God’s presence without divine strength.
God sends Ezekiel to Israel—a people who, like their ancestors, have rebelled against him right up to the present.
The people are stubborn and hard-hearted, but Ezekiel’s job is simply to deliver God’s message: “Thus saith the Lord GOD.”

f.g: Literally “hard of face”—brazen, shameless.
“Lord GOD” renders Adonai YHWH, Ezekiel’s favorite title for God (over 200 times).

chapters.n: Success is not measured by whether they listen. Whether they accept or refuse, they will know a true prophet was among them.

f.g: Refuse, hold back from listening.

f.w: shall know that there hath been a prophet among them

chapters.n: Three times God says “be not afraid.” The people will be as painful as thorns and as dangerous as scorpions, but Ezekiel is not to be intimidated by their words or angry looks.

f.g: A picture of hostile, stinging opposition.

chapters.n: Ezekiel must speak God’s words faithfully, whatever the response.

f.w: thou shalt speak my words unto them

chapters.n: A test of the prophet himself: unlike rebellious Israel, Ezekiel must obey—beginning with eating whatever God gives him.

f.g: Ezekiel must model the obedience Israel lacked.

chapters.n: A hand reaches out to him holding a scroll.

f.g: A scroll.

chapters.n: The scroll is written on both sides—unusual, since scrolls normally had writing only inside—showing the message is full and complete. Its contents: laments, mourning, and woe for Israel.
Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll and then go speak to Israel. Before he can teach God’s word, he must take it fully into himself.
Ezekiel obeys—unlike the rebellious house—and God feeds him the scroll.

f.g: God himself provides what the prophet needs.

chapters.n: Surprisingly, a scroll full of woe tastes sweet as honey. Doing God’s will and receiving his word brings sweetness, even when the message is hard.

f.g: Insides, stomach.

chapters.n: Now he must go and speak God’s words—not his own—to Israel.
Ezekiel is not being sent to foreigners whose language he can’t understand, but to his own people.

f.g: Literally “deep of lip”—an unintelligible language.

chapters.n: Ironically, if God had sent him to foreign nations, they would have listened. Jesus made a similar point about Gentiles who repented more readily than his own people.

f.w: they would have hearkened unto thee

chapters.n: Israel won’t listen to Ezekiel because they won’t listen to God himself. Their rejection is not personal.

f.w: they will not hearken unto me

chapters.n: God makes Ezekiel’s face and forehead as hard as theirs. His name, which means “God strengthens” or “God hardens,” fits this promise.

f.g: A play on the name Ezekiel (Yeḥezqel, “God makes strong”).

chapters.n: His forehead will be harder than flint. He will be able to stand firm against stubborn hearers.

f.g: The hardest stone—perhaps emery or diamond.

chapters.n: Before speaking, Ezekiel must take God’s words into his heart and listen carefully. Inner reception precedes outward preaching.
His specific mission is to the exiles—his own people in captivity—whether they listen or not.

f.g: The Jewish exiles deported to Babylon in 597 BC.

chapters.n: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel up, and he hears a great rushing sound behind him praising the glory of the LORD.

f.w: Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place
f.g: Some scholars suggest a small text change reading “as the glory of the LORD rose from its place.”

chapters.n: The rushing comes from the creatures’ wings and the wheels as the chariot-throne departs.
Ezekiel goes away bitter and agitated—perhaps sharing God’s indignation at Israel’s sin, or overwhelmed by his assignment—but God’s hand is strongly upon him.

f.w: in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit
f.g: Deeply troubled and stirred up.

chapters.n: At Tel-abib, the exiles’ settlement, Ezekiel sits among them stunned for seven days—the traditional length of mourning, and the length of a priest’s ordination.

f.g: “Mound of the flood” or “of spring”; a settlement of Jewish exiles by the Chebar canal (modern Tel Aviv took its name from this verse).

chapters.n: After seven days God speaks to him again.

f.w: at the end of seven days
f.g: A new stage of his commission follows his silent week.

chapters.n: God makes Ezekiel a watchman. Like a sentry on a city wall who warns of approaching danger, a prophet must sound the alarm about spiritual danger.
If Ezekiel fails to warn the wicked, they will still die for their sins, but God will hold Ezekiel responsible. Leaders are accountable for warning those in their care.

f.w: his blood will I require at thine hand

chapters.n: If he warns them and they ignore him, they bear their own guilt, and Ezekiel has saved his own soul.
The duty applies to the righteous too. If a good person turns to sin and the watchman stays silent, both answer for it. Past righteousness does not cancel present wickedness.

f.g: An obstacle or test that reveals a person’s choices.

f.w: his righteousness which he hath done shall not be remembered

chapters.n: But if the watchman warns a righteous person and they heed it, they will live—and the watchman is also saved. Warning is an act of love.

f.w: he shall surely live, because he is warned

chapters.n: God’s hand rests on Ezekiel again, and he is told to go out to the plain for further instruction.

f.g: A valley or open plain near Tel-abib.

chapters.n: There he sees the same glory he saw by the Chebar and falls on his face once more.
The Spirit raises him again and tells him to shut himself in his house—his ministry will begin with dramatic silence.

f.g: His home became the place where elders came to consult him.

chapters.n: Ezekiel will be bound with ropes and unable to go out among the people—whether literally restrained by others or held back by God.

f.g: Cords or ropes.

chapters.n: God will make him unable to speak except when giving God’s word. This silence lasted until news of Jerusalem’s fall reached the exiles years later.

f.g: Unable to speak.

f.w: I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth

chapters.n: When God has a message, he will open Ezekiel’s mouth. Then the choice is the people’s: whoever will hear, let him hear. Jesus used similar words.

f.w: He that heareth, let him hear

chapters.n: Ezekiel begins a series of acted-out prophecies—living object lessons. First he draws Jerusalem on a clay brick, the kind used for writing and building in Babylon.

f.g: A soft clay brick; Babylonians often drew maps and plans on such tablets.

chapters.n: Like a child with toy soldiers, he builds a miniature siege around the drawing: siege wall, ramp, army camps, and battering rams. The exiles watching would grasp that Jerusalem was doomed.

f.g: Build a siege ramp of earth up to the city wall.
Heavy beams used to break city gates and walls.

chapters.n: An iron griddle placed between Ezekiel and the brick represents an unbreakable barrier: God himself has set his face against the city, and prayer will not break through.

f.g: A flat iron plate or griddle used for baking.

f.w: This shall be a sign to the house of Israel

chapters.n: Ezekiel must lie on his left side to “bear” the iniquity of the northern kingdom of Israel—symbolically carrying their guilt and its punishment.

f.g: To carry the burden and consequence of sin, as the scapegoat did symbolically.

chapters.n: Each day stands for a year—390 days for Israel’s long years of sin. Scholars debate exactly which period the 390 years measure.

f.g: The ancient Greek translation reads 190; the meaning of the number is uncertain.

chapters.n: Then he lies on his right side for 40 days, one day for each year of Judah’s iniquity. Forty recalls Israel’s 40 years of wandering in the wilderness.

f.w: I have appointed thee each day for a year

chapters.n: With arm bared like a warrior ready to strike, he faces the model siege and prophesies against Jerusalem.

f.g: A sign of action and power.

chapters.n: God will bind him so he cannot roll over until the siege days are complete. He probably lay in this posture for part of each day, as he also had to prepare food.
He must mix many kinds of grain and legumes into one bread—a famine loaf made from whatever scraps can be found, since no single grain is available in quantity.

f.g: Spelt, a coarse kind of wheat.
Mixing grains was unusual and suggests desperation.

chapters.n: His daily bread ration is only about twenty shekels—roughly 8 ounces (230 grams)—a starvation diet.

f.g: About 8 ounces (230 g).
Food.

chapters.n: His water ration is about two-thirds of a quart (0.6 liter) per day—another sign of siege conditions.

f.w: the sixth part of an hin
f.g: About 2/3 of a quart (0.6 liter).

chapters.n: He is told to bake the bread over human dung as fuel, publicly. This shocks a priest, because it would make the food ritually unclean.

f.g: Dried animal dung was common fuel in the region; human waste was considered defiling.

chapters.n: God explains the sign: in exile, Israel will be forced to eat unclean food among the Gentiles, cut off from the purity laws of their homeland.
Ezekiel protests honestly. As a priest he has always kept the dietary laws and never eaten forbidden or dead animals.

f.w: that which dieth of itself, or is torn in pieces

f.g: Sacrificial meat left too long, which became forbidden.

chapters.n: God mercifully allows him to use cow dung instead—a common fuel. The Lord listens to the sincere concerns of his servants.

f.g: Dried cattle dung, widely used as cooking fuel.

chapters.n: God explains: he will “break the staff of bread” in Jerusalem. People will weigh out food anxiously and drink rationed water in horror.

f.g: Bread as the support of life; to break it means famine.

chapters.n: Lacking food and water, they will stare at one another in shock and waste away because of their sins—just as Lamentations later describes.

f.g: Astonished, stunned.

chapters.n: Ezekiel shaves his head and beard with a sword-sharp blade and weighs the hair into portions. For a priest, shaving was forbidden and shameful—itself a sign of humiliation and mourning.

f.w: upon thine head and upon thy beard

chapters.n: One third he burns in the model city, one third he strikes with the blade around it, and one third he scatters to the wind. These stand for those who will die in the siege, those killed by the sword, and those scattered in exile.

f.w: I will draw out a sword after them

chapters.n: A few hairs are tucked into his garment’s hem—a small remnant God protects.

f.g: Tie them into the fold of his robe for safekeeping.

chapters.n: Even some of the preserved hairs are thrown into the fire. Judgment will continue to touch the survivors too, and fire will spread to all Israel.

f.w: thereof shall a fire come forth into all the house of Israel
f.g: The suffering will touch the whole nation.

chapters.n: God interprets: “This is Jerusalem.” He placed her at the center of the nations to be a light and example.

f.w: I have set it in the midst of the nations

chapters.n: Instead, Jerusalem rebelled against God’s laws more than the surrounding nations did. Greater light brings greater responsibility.

f.g: Laws, rulings.
Decrees, ordinances.

chapters.n: Israel has not even lived up to the moral standard of its pagan neighbors—a stinging charge.

f.g: Probably “been more turbulent/rebellious.”

f.w: neither have done according to the judgments of the nations

chapters.n: “I, even I, am against thee.” God himself will carry out judgment in full view of the nations.

f.w: I, even I, am against thee

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s judgment will be unlike anything before or after—because of her detestable practices.

f.g: Acts God finds detestable, especially idolatry.

chapters.n: Famine will be so extreme that parents and children will eat each other—fulfilling the covenant curses. The survivors will be scattered in every direction.

f.w: the fathers shall eat the sons

chapters.n: God swears by his own life: because the temple has been defiled with idols, he will cut Jerusalem down without pity. Chapter 8 shows these abominations in detail.

f.g: A solemn oath formula; God swears by himself.

chapters.n: Here the meaning of the hair-sign is spelled out: a third will die of plague and famine, a third by the sword, and a third will be scattered and pursued.

f.g: Plague, epidemic disease.

chapters.n: Only after judgment is complete will God’s anger rest. Then the people will recognize that the Lord spoke in his zeal—his passionate, jealous love for his covenant people.

f.g: Or “I will be satisfied”; God’s justice will be fulfilled.
Jealous love, as of a spouse who has been betrayed.

chapters.n: Jerusalem will become a ruin and a byword among the nations.
Her fall will be a warning and an object lesson for other nations—an “instruction.”

f.w: a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment

chapters.n: Famine is pictured as deadly arrows God shoots, breaking the “staff of bread.”
Famine, wild animals, plague, bloodshed, and sword—the classic covenant curses—will sweep the land.
A new message from the Lord begins—the usual way Ezekiel marks a new oracle.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: This formula appears about 50 times in Ezekiel.

chapters.n: Ezekiel must turn toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them, because the hilltops were where idol worship flourished.

f.g: Ezekiel’s typical phrase for directing a prophecy at a target.

chapters.n: The whole landscape—mountains, hills, ravines, valleys—hears that God will bring a sword and destroy the “high places,” hilltop shrines for idols.

f.g: Hilltop shrines where Israelites worshiped idols or worshiped the Lord in forbidden ways.

chapters.n: Altars will be wrecked, incense stands smashed, and worshippers will die in front of the idols that could not save them.

f.g: Probably incense altars or sun-pillars.
Ezekiel’s word gillulim is a scornful term, possibly “dung-gods.”

chapters.n: Corpses and bones scattered around the altars will make these shrines unclean—an ironic end to false worship.

f.w: I will scatter your bones round about your altars

chapters.n: Every town will be ruined and every idol shrine destroyed. All the work of human hands in false worship will be wiped out.
The key refrain of Ezekiel appears: “ye shall know that I am the LORD.” It occurs over 60 times. The purpose of judgment is that people recognize who God truly is.

f.w: ye shall know that I am the LORD

chapters.n: Yet a remnant will survive and be scattered among the nations. Judgment is never God’s final word.
In exile the survivors will remember God. Strikingly, God says he is “broken” by their unfaithful hearts—he feels the pain of their betrayal. They will come to loathe their own sins.

f.g: Or “I was crushed/grieved”—God’s personal anguish over Israel’s infidelity.
A picture of covenant unfaithfulness, like a spouse who cheats.

chapters.n: They will realize God’s warnings were not empty threats.

f.w: I have not said in vain

chapters.n: Ezekiel is told to clap and stamp—gestures of grief or emphasis—and cry “Alas!” over Israel’s sins and their coming end by sword, famine, and plague.

f.w: Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot
f.g: Dramatic gestures accompanying the message.

chapters.n: No one will escape: those far away die of plague, those nearby by the sword, and those trapped in the city by famine.
The dead will lie beside the very idols they worshipped—on hilltops, under green trees and oaks, where they offered “sweet savour” to false gods instead of to the Lord.

f.g: The pleasing aroma of an offering, meant only for the Lord.

chapters.n: The land will be more desolate than the wilderness of Diblath. Then they will know the Lord.

f.g: Probably Riblah in Syria, where Zedekiah was judged; a scribal r/d confusion is likely.

chapters.n: Another message arrives. Chapter 7 is a poem of alarm, with short, hammering phrases like a warning bell.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: “An end! The end has come” on the whole land of Israel, in every direction. Amos had used the same stark word about the northern kingdom.

f.w: An end, the end is come
the four corners of the land
f.g: The whole land, from every direction.

chapters.n: God will judge Judah by its own ways and repay it for its detestable practices. Consequences match choices.
Judah’s own sins will be in its midst, visible to all. Through the consequences they will finally recognize the Lord.

f.w: mine eye shall not spare thee

chapters.n: A unique, unprecedented disaster is arriving.

f.g: A one-of-a-kind calamity; some manuscripts read “disaster after disaster.”

chapters.n: The end is personified as an enemy who has been “watching”—lying in wait—and now arrives. In Hebrew, “end” (qets) and “awake/watch” (heqits) make a wordplay.

f.g: Literally “it has awakened against you.”

chapters.n: Doom (or “the morning”) has come; the day of trouble is near—not the joyful shouting of harvest festivals on the mountains.

f.g: The Hebrew word is uncertain; possibly “doom” or “your turn.”

f.w: the sounding again of the mountains
f.g: Probably joyful shouts, as at harvest or festival time.

chapters.n: God will soon pour out his fury and judge according to their ways—echoing verse 3.
A new title appears: “the LORD that smiteth.” Israel will recognize God as the one who strikes when they refuse correction.

“The rod has blossomed, pride has budded”: wickedness has come to full flower and is ready to bear fruit—or the “rod” of punishment (Babylon) is ready. Compare Aaron’s budding rod, which once confirmed God’s chosen priesthood.
Violence has grown into a rod that will punish wickedness. Nothing of their wealth or crowds will remain, and the destruction will be so complete there will be no one left to mourn.

f.w: neither shall there be wailing for them

chapters.n: Normal business means nothing now. Buyers shouldn’t celebrate their bargain, nor sellers mourn their loss, because all property is about to be lost anyway.

f.w: let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn

chapters.n: Land sold under the law would usually return to its family in the Jubilee year—but not this time. Exile will undo all transactions.

f.w: the seller shall not return to that which is sold
f.g: Under the Jubilee law, sold family land was restored every fiftieth year.

chapters.n: The trumpet sounds a call to arms, but no one goes out to fight—courage is gone because God’s wrath is upon them.
The sword outside the city and famine and plague inside—there is no safe place.
Survivors will hide in the mountains, moaning like doves, each mourning for his own sins.

f.g: Doves’ cooing was compared to mourning.

chapters.n: Terror will drain their strength: hands go limp, and knees turn to water.

f.w: all knees shall be weak as water
f.g: Possibly a vivid idiom for losing bladder control from fear.

chapters.n: They will wear sackcloth and shave their heads in mourning, covered with horror and shame.

f.g: Shaving the head was a sign of mourning.

chapters.n: People will throw their silver and gold into the streets as worthless. Wealth, which had become their stumbling block and even the material of their idols, cannot save them in the day of the Lord.

f.w: their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them

chapters.n: God gave them beautiful jewelry, but they used it to make idols. So he will take it away from them.

f.g: Their gold and silver jewelry—or possibly the temple, Israel’s glorious ornament.

f.w: they made the images of their abominations

chapters.n: Their treasures will go to foreigners as plunder, who will profane them.

f.g: Foreigners—here the Babylonians.

chapters.n: God will turn his face away, allowing robbers to enter and defile his “secret place”—the temple’s Holy of Holies.

f.g: His treasured place—the temple and its inner sanctuary.

f.w: My face will I turn also from them

chapters.n: Prepare a chain for captives, because the land is full of bloodshed and violence.

f.g: Prepare chains for prisoners being led into exile.

chapters.n: God will bring the most ruthless of nations to take their homes. Their proud strength will end, and their sanctuaries will be defiled.

f.g: The Babylonians, known for ruthlessness.

chapters.n: Terror comes; they will look for peace but find none—the false prophets’ promises of “peace” will fail.

f.w: they shall seek peace, and there shall be none

chapters.n: Disaster on disaster, rumor on rumor. Desperate people will seek a vision from a prophet, instruction from a priest, or advice from elders—but none will have answers.

f.w: the law shall perish from the priest

f.g: Elders.

chapters.n: King, prince, and commoner alike will despair. God will judge them by their own standards, and they will know he is the LORD.

f.g: According to what they deserve.

chapters.n: About fourteen months after his call (about 592 BC), Judah’s elders in exile are sitting in Ezekiel’s house when God’s power falls on him. Chapters 8–11 form one long vision.

f.w: the sixth year, in the sixth month
f.g: Of King Jehoiachin’s exile—about September 592 BC.

f.w: the elders of Judah sat before me

chapters.n: Ezekiel sees a fiery, radiant figure like the one on the throne in chapter 1.

A hand grabs him by the hair, and the Spirit carries him in vision to Jerusalem’s temple. There, at the north gate, stands an idol called “the image of jealousy” because it provokes God’s jealous love for his people.

f.w: took me by a lock of mine head

f.g: Perhaps an image of the goddess Asherah, like the one King Manasseh once set in the temple.

chapters.n: God’s glory is still present in the temple, just as Ezekiel saw it in the plain—for now. These chapters trace its slow departure.

f.w: according to the vision that I saw in the plain

chapters.n: Looking north, Ezekiel sees the idol standing at the gate by the altar—right at the entrance to God’s house.

f.g: A northern gate of the inner court, near the great altar.

chapters.n: These abominations are driving God away from his own sanctuary. “But you will see even worse.” The vision builds in four escalating scenes.

f.w: that I should go far off from my sanctuary

chapters.n: At the entrance to the court Ezekiel sees a hole in the wall.

f.g: One of the temple courtyards.

chapters.n: Told to dig through it, he finds a hidden door—secret sin concealed inside the house of God.

f.g: An image of exposing what is hidden.

chapters.n: He is told to go in and see the wicked things being done there.

f.g: Detestable acts of idolatry.

chapters.n: Inside, the walls are carved with unclean creatures and idols—likely Egyptian-style animal gods—that the law forbade Israel to worship.
Seventy elders—the very number Moses appointed to lead Israel—are offering incense to these images. Among them is Jaazaniah, son of Shaphan, from a family that had otherwise been faithful.

f.g: Josiah’s scribe; his sons supported Jeremiah.
A pan for burning incense.

chapters.n: They worship in the dark, each in his own room of images, telling themselves that the Lord doesn’t see and has abandoned the land. Secret sin often begins with the belief that God isn’t watching.

f.g: Rooms decorated with idolatrous images; also suggests their private thoughts.

chapters.n: “Turn again, and you will see greater abominations.”

f.g: The escalation continues to a third scene.

chapters.n: At the north gate of the temple, women sit weeping for Tammuz, a Mesopotamian fertility god whose death was mourned each summer.

f.g: Babylonian Dumuzi, a god of vegetation believed to die and revive with the seasons; the fourth month of the Jewish calendar still bears his name.

chapters.n: “Have you seen this? You will see still greater abominations.”

f.g: God asks Ezekiel to fully take in what he is seeing.

chapters.n: The worst scene, in the inner court right at the temple door: about twenty-five men turn their backs on the Lord’s house and bow to the rising sun in the east—an act of total rejection.

f.w: with their backs toward the temple of the LORD
between the porch and the altar
f.g: The area reserved for priests.

chapters.n: Idolatry isn’t a minor thing: it goes hand in hand with filling the land with violence. “They put the branch to their nose” is an obscure idiom, probably a pagan ritual gesture or an insulting gesture toward God.

f.w: they put the branch to their nose
f.g: Meaning uncertain; possibly a ritual act in sun worship, or an obscene insult to God.

chapters.n: Therefore God will act without pity. Even if they cry loudly to him, he will not answer—prayer without repentance does not move heaven.

f.w: though they cry in mine ears with a loud voice, yet will I not hear them

chapters.n: Continuing the vision, God calls loudly for the city’s appointed executioners to come forward with their weapons. These are heavenly agents of judgment.

f.w: them that have charge over the city
f.g: Those appointed to punish the city—angelic executioners.

chapters.n: Six men arrive from the north with weapons, and a seventh dressed in priestly linen carries a scribe’s writing kit. They stand by the bronze altar, where judgment will begin.

f.g: Linen was worn by priests and heavenly messengers.
A scribe’s case holding pens and ink.

chapters.n: God’s glory begins to leave. It rises from above the cherub over the ark and moves to the temple’s doorway—the first step of its departure.

f.w: the glory of the God of Israel was gone up from the cherub

f.g: The doorway or entrance of the temple building.

chapters.n: Before any judgment falls, the man in linen must mark the foreheads of all who grieve over the city’s sins. God knows and protects his faithful, even in a wicked city.

f.w: set a mark upon the foreheads
f.g: The Hebrew word for “mark” is taw, the last letter of the alphabet, written in ancient script like an X or cross.

chapters.n: The six executioners are to follow and strike without pity.

No one unmarked is spared—but no one with the mark is touched. Judgment begins at God’s sanctuary, with the elders who were worshipping idols there. Peter later taught that judgment begins at the house of God.

f.w: the ancient men which were before the house

chapters.n: They are to defile the temple with the dead—it has already been defiled by idolatry—and then go out into the city.

f.g: Dead bodies made a place ritually unclean.

chapters.n: Left alone among the slain, Ezekiel falls on his face and pleads for the remnant of Israel. Like Abraham and Moses, the prophet intercedes for the people.

f.g: Remnant, those who remain.

chapters.n: God answers that the guilt of both Israel and Judah is enormous. The land is full of bloodshed and injustice, and the people even say God has abandoned them and cannot see.

f.g: Perversion of justice.

chapters.n: Because of this, God will hold back his pity and bring their own conduct back upon their heads.

f.w: recompense their way upon their head
f.g: Make them bear the consequences of their own actions.

chapters.n: The man in linen reports: “I have done as you commanded.” The faithful have been marked and protected—the vision ends with obedience completed.

f.w: I have done as thou hast commanded me

chapters.n: Ezekiel again sees the sapphire throne above the platform over the cherubim—the same chariot-throne from chapter 1, now at the temple.

f.g: Plural of cherub (the KJV adds an extra English -s to the Hebrew plural -im).

chapters.n: The man in linen is told to take burning coals from between the wheels and scatter them over Jerusalem. Coals that purified Isaiah’s lips now bring judgment on the city.
The cherubim stand on the south side of the temple, and a cloud fills the inner court.

f.w: on the right side of the house
f.g: The south side, as one faces east.

f.w: the cloud filled the inner court

chapters.n: God’s glory rises from the cherub and pauses at the threshold; the temple fills with cloud and brightness. At Solomon’s dedication the glory filled the temple; now it is preparing to leave.

f.w: the house was filled with the cloud

chapters.n: The cherubim’s wings sound like God’s own voice, heard all the way to the outer court.

f.w: the voice of the Almighty God

chapters.n: The man in linen goes in and stands beside a wheel to take the fire.

f.g: From the heart of the fiery throne-chariot.

chapters.n: A cherub reaches into the fire and places coals in the man’s hands, and he goes out to scatter them. The burning of Jerusalem in 586 BC fulfilled this vision.

f.w: put it into the hands of him that was clothed with linen

chapters.n: Ezekiel notes again that the cherubim have human-like hands under their wings.

f.w: the form of a man's hand

chapters.n: He sees the four wheels beside the four cherubim, gleaming like a precious stone.
All four wheels look alike, each like a wheel set within another.

f.w: a wheel had been in the midst of a wheel

chapters.n: They move in any direction without turning, following wherever the lead faces.

f.g: Whichever way the front faced, or wherever the leading cherub went.

chapters.n: Here even the cherubim’s bodies, backs, hands, and wings—not just the wheels—are covered with eyes, symbolizing perfect awareness.
Ezekiel hears the wheels called “the whirling wheels”—a name suggesting swift, storm-like motion.

f.g: Hebrew galgal—“whirl” or “whirlwind,” a different word from the ordinary wheel.

chapters.n: Each cherub has four faces. Here the ox face of chapter 1 is called “the face of a cherub,” perhaps because a winged bull was a familiar cherub image.
The cherubim rise. Ezekiel now realizes these are the same living creatures he saw by the Chebar.

f.w: This is the living creature that I saw by the river of Chebar

chapters.n: The wheels move with the cherubim and stay right beside them as they rise.
When they stand or rise, the wheels do too, because the same spirit moves them.

f.w: the spirit of the living creature was in them

chapters.n: A sobering moment: God’s glory leaves the temple’s doorway and mounts the cherubim chariot. The Lord is withdrawing from the house his people defiled.

f.w: the glory of the LORD departed
f.g: This recalls the name Ichabod, “the glory is departed.”

chapters.n: The cherubim rise and pause at the temple’s east gate, with God’s glory above them. Each stage is slow, as if God is reluctant to leave.

f.w: the east gate of the LORD's house
f.g: The main entrance; the glory later returns by this same gate.

chapters.n: Ezekiel confirms: these are the creatures he saw beneath the God of Israel by the Chebar—now he knows they are cherubim, guardians of God’s holy presence.

f.w: I knew that they were the cherubims

chapters.n: Each has four faces, four wings, and human-like hands under the wings.
Their faces are the very same as by the Chebar, and each moves straight forward. The same God who appeared to the exiles is leaving Jerusalem—his presence is now with the faithful in exile.

f.w: they went every one straight forward

chapters.n: The Spirit carries Ezekiel to the temple’s east gate, where twenty-five leaders are gathered, including Jaazaniah son of Azur (a different man from 8:11) and Pelatiah son of Benaiah.

f.g: Civic leaders and officials of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: These men plot evil and give the city wicked advice.

f.g: Plan wrongdoing.

chapters.n: They say: “Destruction isn’t near; let’s build houses. This city is the cooking pot and we are the meat”—meaning they are the choice cuts, safe inside the walls, while the exiles were the scraps thrown away.

f.w: It is not near; let us build houses
f.g: Possibly the opposite of Jeremiah’s advice to the exiles to build houses in Babylon.
A large cooking pot.

chapters.n: God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against them—twice, for emphasis.

f.g: The repetition stresses urgency.

chapters.n: The Spirit falls on Ezekiel. God knows every thought that crosses their minds.

f.w: I know the things that come into your mind

chapters.n: These leaders have filled Jerusalem’s streets with murdered people through their injustice.
God turns their saying around: the only “meat” safe in the pot is the innocent people they killed. The leaders themselves will be dragged out.

f.g: The victims, not the leaders, are the true choice portion.

chapters.n: They feared the sword, so the sword will come upon them.
God will remove them from the city and hand them over to foreigners for judgment.

f.w: deliver you into the hands of strangers

chapters.n: They will die at Israel’s border. This was fulfilled when Nebuchadnezzar executed Judah’s leaders at Riblah, at the northern edge of the land.

f.w: I will judge you in the border of Israel

chapters.n: Jerusalem will not protect them like a pot protects meat; judgment will meet them at the border.

f.w: This city shall not be your caldron
f.g: Their false security is exposed.

chapters.n: They will know the Lord, because instead of following his laws they copied the ways of the surrounding nations.

f.w: have done after the manners of the heathen

chapters.n: As Ezekiel prophesies in vision, Pelatiah suddenly dies—perhaps at the same moment in Jerusalem. Shaken, Ezekiel falls down and cries out: will God destroy the whole remnant?

f.g: His name ironically means “The LORD rescues.”

f.w: wilt thou make a full end of the remnant

chapters.n: God answers with a new message—one of hope.

f.w: Again the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: A turn from judgment to promise.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s residents scorn the exiles: “They are far from the Lord; the land is ours now.” But God says the exiles are Ezekiel’s true brothers and the real heirs of the promise.

f.w: Get you far from the LORD
f.g: They assumed being in Jerusalem meant being close to God.

f.w: unto us is this land given in possession

chapters.n: One of the most comforting verses in Ezekiel: though God scattered them, he himself will be “a little sanctuary” for them in exile. God’s presence is not limited to a building or a land.

f.g: Or “a sanctuary for a little while.” Jewish tradition connects this to the synagogue.

chapters.n: God promises to gather the scattered and give them the land of Israel again—a theme of latter-day gathering that Latter-day Saints emphasize.

f.r: Ezekiel 36:24; Jeremiah 32:37; 1 Nephi 22:12; Articles of Faith 1:10

chapters.n: When they return, they will remove all the idols and abominations from the land.

f.w: they shall take away all the detestable things

chapters.n: The heart of the promise: God will give his people one heart and a new spirit, replacing a stony, unfeeling heart with a heart of flesh—responsive and alive. This is a picture of spiritual rebirth.

f.w: I will put a new spirit within you

chapters.n: The new heart leads to obedience, and obedience restores the covenant relationship: “they shall be my people, and I will be their God.”

f.w: they shall be my people, and I will be their God

chapters.n: But those whose hearts stay devoted to their idols will receive the consequences of their own conduct.

f.w: whose heart walketh after the heart of their detestable things
f.g: Whose loyalty stays with their idols.

chapters.n: The cherubim lift their wings, with the wheels and God’s glory above them. The departure continues.

f.w: the glory of the God of Israel was over them

chapters.n: God’s glory leaves the city entirely and rests on the mountain east of Jerusalem—the Mount of Olives. Prophecy and the New Testament connect this mountain with the Lord’s coming again.

f.w: the mountain which is on the east side of the city
f.g: The Mount of Olives.

chapters.n: The Spirit returns Ezekiel in vision to the exiles in Babylonia, and the vision ends.

f.g: Babylonia.

chapters.n: Ezekiel tells the exiles everything the Lord showed him—both the judgment on Jerusalem and the promise of a new heart.

f.w: all the things that the LORD had shewed me

chapters.n: A new message introduces another acted-out sign.

f.w: The word of the LORD also came unto me

chapters.n: Ezekiel lives among people who have eyes and ears but refuse to see or hear spiritual truth. Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Jesus used the same image.

f.w: which have eyes to see, and see not

chapters.n: He must pack an exile’s bag in broad daylight and move from place to place while people watch. Perhaps the drama will make them think.

f.g: Baggage for exile—the few things a deportee could carry.

f.w: it may be they will consider
f.g: God still hopes they will reflect and repent.

chapters.n: He sets his bag out by day and leaves in the evening like someone being marched off as a captive.

f.g: In the evening.

chapters.n: He must dig through the wall of his house—mud brick in Babylon—and carry his belongings out through the hole.

f.g: Babylonian houses were mud brick, easy to dig through.

chapters.n: He carries the bag on his shoulder at dusk with his face covered so he cannot see the ground. Ezekiel himself is God’s sign to Israel.

f.g: A detail pointing to a blinded king (v. 13).

chapters.n: Ezekiel obeys every detail. A prophet’s obedience is part of his message.

f.w: I did so as I was commanded

chapters.n: The next morning the Lord explains the sign.

f.g: After the people had watched the night’s performance.

chapters.n: The people had asked, “What are you doing?” His strange actions got their attention.
The message concerns the “prince” in Jerusalem—King Zedekiah—and all Israel there.

f.g: A prophetic oracle; also a pun on the bag Ezekiel carried.
Ezekiel calls Zedekiah “prince,” perhaps because many still regarded the exiled Jehoiachin as the true king.

chapters.n: “I am your sign”: just as Ezekiel acted it out, the people of Jerusalem will be carried off into captivity.
Zedekiah will try to escape at night through a hole in the wall, carrying his things, his face covered. This happened exactly when Jerusalem fell: the king fled by night through a gap in the wall.

f.w: the prince that is among them shall bear upon his shoulder in the twilight

chapters.n: A striking prophecy: Zedekiah will be taken to Babylon yet will not see it, though he dies there. It was fulfilled when the Babylonians blinded him before taking him to Babylon.

f.w: yet shall he not see it, though he shall die there
My net also will I spread upon him

chapters.n: His bodyguards and troops will be scattered, and the sword will pursue them.

f.g: His troops.

chapters.n: Scattered among the nations, they will finally recognize the Lord.
God will spare a few survivors so that, among the nations, they can testify that Israel’s fall was due to its own sins and not to God’s weakness.

f.w: that they may declare all their abominations among the heathen

chapters.n: Another message and another sign.

f.w: Moreover the word of the LORD came to me

chapters.n: Ezekiel must eat and drink while shaking with fear, acting out the terror of the coming siege.

f.g: Trembling, shuddering.
Anxiety, worry.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s people will eat and drink with anxiety and horror because their land will be stripped bare, all because of the violence of its people.

f.g: Horror, dismay.

f.w: because of the violence of all them that dwell therein

chapters.n: Populated towns will become ruins and the land a wasteland.

f.w: the cities that are inhabited shall be laid waste

chapters.n: Another message, this time answering a popular saying.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: People had a proverb: “Time goes on and every vision comes to nothing.” Because predicted judgment hadn’t happened yet, they assumed it never would.

f.w: The days are prolonged, and every vision faileth

chapters.n: God will put an end to that proverb. The new one will be: “The days are near, and every vision will be fulfilled.”

f.g: The fulfillment of every prophecy.

chapters.n: False visions and flattering fortune-telling will cease in Israel.

f.g: Smooth, comforting predictions people wanted to hear.

chapters.n: God declares that what he says will happen—no more delay. It will come in their own lifetime.

f.w: the word that I shall speak shall come to pass

chapters.n: Another message responds to a second excuse.

f.w: Again the word of the LORD came to me

chapters.n: Others admitted the prophecies might be true but said they were about the distant future, not them. It was a way of avoiding personal repentance.

f.w: he prophesieth of the times that are far off

chapters.n: God replies: none of his words will be delayed any longer. What he has spoken will be done. Within six years Jerusalem fell.

f.w: There shall none of my words be prolonged any more

chapters.n: A new message targets the false prophets who were misleading Israel—a serious problem in Ezekiel’s and Jeremiah’s day.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Ezekiel must speak against prophets who invent messages “out of their own hearts.” Real prophecy comes from God, not human imagination.

f.w: that prophesy out of their own hearts

chapters.n: Woe to foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and have actually seen nothing.

f.g: Rely on their own ideas rather than God’s Spirit.
Hebrew nabal—morally foolish, not just unintelligent.

chapters.n: These prophets are like jackals prowling in ruins—scavengers who thrive on disaster instead of preventing it.

f.g: Jackals or foxes living among ruins.

chapters.n: A true prophet would stand in the breach of a broken wall to defend the people, calling them to repentance. These prophets never repaired the gaps.

f.w: Ye have not gone up into the gaps

f.g: Repaired the wall.

chapters.n: They claim, “The LORD says,” though God never sent them, and then expect their words to come true.

f.w: the LORD hath not sent them

chapters.n: God confronts them directly: haven’t you seen false visions and spoken lies while claiming God said them?

f.g: Even though I have not spoken.

chapters.n: Because they spoke falsehood, God is against them.
Their punishment is to be cut off from God’s people: excluded from the council, left out of Israel’s registry, and barred from returning to the land.

f.w: neither shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel

chapters.n: Their great crime was promising “Peace” when there was no peace. Their message was like a weak wall covered with whitewash to make it look solid.

f.w: Peace; and there was no peace

f.g: Whitewash or plaster that only covers cracks without strengthening anything.

chapters.n: Tell the whitewashers the wall will fall. Rain, hail, and wind will strike it. Compare Jesus’s parable of the houses built on rock and sand.

f.w: there shall be an overflowing shower

chapters.n: When it falls, people will ask, “Where is all that whitewash you put on it?” Comforting lies collapse when tested.

f.g: Where is your plaster now?

chapters.n: God himself is the storm that tears the wall down.
The wall will fall down to its foundations, burying those who whitewashed it.

f.w: the foundation thereof shall be discovered
f.g: Its foundation will be exposed.

chapters.n: God will finish his judgment: “The wall is no more, neither those who whitewashed it.”

f.g: Both the false hope and those who promoted it will be gone.

chapters.n: The meaning is made plain: the prophets who promised peace for Jerusalem.
Now Ezekiel turns to women who also invent prophecies from their own hearts.

f.g: Women acting as false prophetesses or sorceresses.

chapters.n: They sew magic bands for wrists and make veils for every head size—tools of sorcery used to “hunt souls,” controlling people’s lives through fear and superstition.

f.g: Probably magic bands or charms tied on wrists.
Veils or head coverings used in their rituals.

chapters.n: For handfuls of barley and bits of bread they profane God’s name, pronouncing death on the innocent and life on the guilty. Spiritual deception for small payment is especially wicked.

f.w: for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread

chapters.n: God is against their magic bands. He will rip them away and free the people they trapped like birds.

f.g: Like birds caught in a trap; possibly “like birds.”

chapters.n: He will tear their veils and rescue his people from their power.

f.w: deliver my people out of your hand

chapters.n: Their lies discouraged the righteous and encouraged the wicked to stay in sin by promising them safety. False teaching often reverses God’s values.

f.w: strengthened the hands of the wicked

chapters.n: Their false visions and divinations will end, and God will free his people.

f.g: Practice fortune-telling.

chapters.n: Some of Israel’s elders in exile come and sit before Ezekiel, apparently wanting a word from the Lord.
God speaks to Ezekiel about these visitors.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: God reveals what lies behind their outward piety.

chapters.n: Outwardly they seek God, but they have set up idols in their hearts. Their inner loyalties trip them up. Should God answer people like that?

f.w: set up their idols in their heart
f.g: An idol can be anything we love or trust more than God.
Something that causes a person to trip and fall into sin.

chapters.n: Anyone who comes to a prophet while clinging to heart-idols will get an answer that matches those idols—God will respond to the real condition of their heart.

f.w: according to the multitude of his idols
f.g: In keeping with, or because of, their idols.

chapters.n: God’s aim is to “take hold of” Israel’s hearts—to win them back, since their idols have made them strangers to him.

f.w: take the house of Israel in their own heart
f.g: Grip their hearts; confront them inwardly.
Alienated, made strangers.

chapters.n: The cure is plain: repent, turn away from your idols, and turn your faces from your abominations.
This applies to Israelites and to foreigners living among them alike. God himself will answer such a person.

f.w: the stranger that sojourneth in Israel
f.g: A resident foreigner, who was also under God’s law.

f.w: I the LORD will answer him by myself
f.g: God will respond directly—with judgment rather than words.

chapters.n: God will oppose that person and make him a warning example and a byword, cut off from his people.

If a prophet is drawn into giving such people the comfortable answer they want, God permits that deception and will judge the prophet too. Those who refuse truth may be given over to their own delusions.

f.w: I the LORD have deceived that prophet
f.g: Hebrew idiom: God allows it as judgment.

chapters.n: Both the inquirer and the false prophet will bear the same punishment—both chose to prefer lies to truth.

f.w: the punishment of the prophet shall be even as the punishment of him that seeketh unto him

chapters.n: The purpose of judgment is restoration: that Israel stops straying, is cleansed, and becomes God’s people again.

f.w: that they may be my people, and I may be their God

chapters.n: A new message about whether the righteous can save others.

f.w: The word of the LORD came again to me

chapters.n: When a land sins grievously, God may send famine, cutting off both people and animals.

f.w: break the staff of the bread

chapters.n: Even if Noah, Daniel, and Job—famous examples of righteousness—lived there, their goodness would save only themselves. Righteousness can’t be transferred to others who refuse to repent.

f.g: Noah and Job were ancient righteous men; Daniel was Ezekiel’s contemporary in Babylon, though some scholars think an ancient hero named Danel is meant.

chapters.n: Or if God sends wild animals to depopulate the land so no one can pass through…

f.g: Harmful, dangerous wild animals.

chapters.n: …even these three could not save their own sons or daughters; only they would survive.

f.w: they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters
f.g: In contrast, Noah’s family was saved with him.

chapters.n: Or if God commands a sword to sweep through the land…
…the same: only the righteous themselves would be rescued.

f.w: they only shall be delivered themselves
f.g: Each person stands before God for himself.

chapters.n: Or if God sends plague and bloodshed…

f.g: Deadly epidemic.

chapters.n: …Noah, Daniel, and Job could only save their own lives by their righteousness. The fourfold repetition drives the point home.

f.w: they shall but deliver their own souls by their righteousness

chapters.n: How much worse for Jerusalem, which will face all four judgments together—sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague.
Surprisingly, some survivors—sons and daughters—will come out and arrive among the exiles. When the exiles see how wicked they are, they will understand why God judged Jerusalem.

f.w: a remnant that shall be brought forth

f.g: Consoled—by understanding that God acted justly.

chapters.n: Seeing the survivors’ conduct, the exiles will know that God did nothing without cause. God’s judgments are never arbitrary.

f.w: I have not done without cause

chapters.n: A short parable begins. Israel was often pictured as a vine God planted; here the image takes an unexpected turn.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: What makes a vine’s wood better than any forest tree? Grapevines are valuable only for their fruit; their wood is twisted and weak.

f.g: The grapevine.

chapters.n: You can’t build anything from vine wood—not even a peg to hang a pot on.

f.g: A peg.

chapters.n: It’s only good for fuel. And after the fire chars both ends and the middle, it’s good for even less. Judah had been “burned” already by earlier Babylonian invasions.

f.w: the fire devoureth both the ends of it
f.g: Perhaps Judah’s earlier losses in 605 and 597 BC.
Suitable, fit.

chapters.n: If it was useless when whole, how much more after it has been burned! A vine that bears no fruit has no other purpose.

f.w: when it was whole, it was meet for no work

chapters.n: So it is with Jerusalem: a fruitless vine fit only for burning. Its value depended on producing the fruit of righteousness.

f.w: so will I give the inhabitants of Jerusalem

chapters.n: Some have escaped one fire, but another will catch them. Survivors of earlier invasions will not escape the final one.

f.w: they shall go out from one fire, and another fire shall devour them

chapters.n: The land will be made desolate because they were unfaithful.

f.g: Hebrew ma‘al—unfaithfulness, a breach of trust against God.

chapters.n: Chapter 16 is Ezekiel’s longest prophecy—an allegory of Jerusalem as an abandoned baby girl whom God rescues, raises, and marries, but who becomes unfaithful. Its language is blunt because covenant betrayal is serious.

f.w: Again the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Ezekiel’s task is to make Jerusalem face honestly what she has done.

f.w: cause Jerusalem to know her abominations

chapters.n: Jerusalem was originally a Canaanite city (it was a Jebusite town before David took it). Calling her parents an Amorite and a Hittite means: by nature, you are no better than the pagans around you.

f.w: thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother an Hittite
f.g: Amorites and Hittites were among the peoples of Canaan before Israel.

chapters.n: At birth the baby received none of the ordinary care: no cutting of the cord, no washing, no rubbing with salt (a common ancient practice), no wrapping in cloths.

f.g: Newborns were rubbed with salt, thought to cleanse and strengthen the skin.
Wrapped snugly in strips of cloth.

chapters.n: No one cared enough to do these things. The newborn was thrown out into an open field to die—a cruel practice known in the ancient world.

f.w: cast out in the open field
f.g: Infant exposure—abandoning unwanted babies.

chapters.n: God passed by, saw her struggling in her own blood, and said, “Live!” twice. This is grace: life given to someone who could do nothing for herself.

f.w: I have caused thee to multiply

f.w: I spread my skirt over thee
f.g: A symbolic act of betrothal and protection.

f.w: entered into a covenant with thee

chapters.n: He washed and anointed her. Washing and anointing are covenant images that also suggest preparation for holy service.

f.w: I throughly washed away thy blood

chapters.n: He dressed her in embroidered clothing, fine leather sandals, linen, and costly fabric—the language even echoes the materials of the tabernacle.

f.g: Fine leather—the same material used to cover the tabernacle.
Embroidered cloth.

chapters.n: He adorned her with bracelets and a necklace, like a bride.
A nose ring, earrings, and a beautiful crown completed her royal adornment.

f.g: Literally a nose ring, a common bridal ornament.

chapters.n: She ate the finest food and became exceedingly beautiful, rising to be a kingdom—the glory years of David and Solomon.

f.w: thou didst prosper into a kingdom

chapters.n: Her fame spread among the nations, but her beauty was a gift—perfect because of the splendor God had given her.

f.w: my comeliness, which I had put upon thee
f.g: Her beauty came from God, not from herself.

chapters.n: The turning point: she trusted in her own beauty instead of the Giver and gave herself to every passerby. In the prophets, prostitution symbolizes idolatry—giving to false gods the love owed to God.

f.w: thou didst trust in thine own beauty

chapters.n: She used the very clothing God gave her to decorate idol shrines—turning gifts against the Giver. Such a thing should never have happened.

f.g: Various colors.

chapters.n: She melted down her gold and silver jewelry—God’s gifts—to make idols in human form.

f.g: Male idols.

f.w: of my gold and of my silver

chapters.n: She clothed these idols with her embroidered garments and offered them God’s oil and incense.

f.g: Offerings that belonged to God.

chapters.n: Even the food God provided she offered to idols as a pleasing aroma.
Worst of all, she sacrificed the children she had borne to God—a horrific practice of Molech worship. Were her other betrayals not enough?

f.w: thy sons and thy daughters, whom thou hast borne unto me

chapters.n: God calls them “my children”—the children of his covenant—slain and offered in fire to idols.

f.w: to cause them to pass through the fire

chapters.n: In all this she forgot where she came from—the helpless, abandoned baby God had saved. Forgetting God’s past mercy leads to ingratitude and sin.

f.w: thou hast not remembered the days of thy youth

chapters.n: God breaks in with a cry of grief: “Woe, woe to you!”

f.g: A cry of lament as much as of judgment.

chapters.n: She built a shrine-platform and set up high places in every public street.

f.g: A raised mound or platform, probably for idol worship.

chapters.n: Idol shrines stood at every crossroads, and she offered herself to all who passed—her idolatry was open and constant.

f.w: at every head of the way
f.g: At the beginning of every road or intersection.

chapters.n: She made alliances with Egypt, adopting its gods—treaties with nations meant honoring their deities, so foreign politics became spiritual unfaithfulness.

f.g: A crude image of Egypt’s power and allure.

chapters.n: So God reduced her territory and handed her to her enemies, the Philistines—who were themselves embarrassed by her conduct.

f.g: Reduced her allotted portion or territory.
Philistine cities; even pagans were ashamed of Judah’s behavior.

chapters.n: She also courted Assyria, yet never felt satisfied. Idolatry never fills the emptiness it promises to fill.

f.g: Never satisfied.

chapters.n: She extended her unfaithfulness to Babylon (Chaldea), still unsatisfied.

f.g: Babylon.

chapters.n: “How weak your heart is!”—her will had no strength to resist temptation; she acted like a brazen, domineering woman.

f.g: Possibly “how feverish/lovesick your heart is.”
Bold and shameless.

chapters.n: She built shrines at every crossroads, yet unlike a prostitute she did not even charge a fee.

f.g: She refused payment.

chapters.n: She is like an adulterous wife who prefers strangers to her own husband.
Prostitutes are paid, but Jerusalem pays her lovers! Judah actually sent tribute to foreign powers to win their favor.

f.w: thou givest thy gifts to all thy lovers

chapters.n: She is the reverse of other women: she pays instead of being paid. Her folly is beyond reason.

f.g: You are the opposite.

chapters.n: Now comes the verdict: “Hear the word of the LORD.”

f.g: A stark title for covenant-breaking Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Because of her shameful idolatry, her lovers, her idols, and the blood of her children…

f.g: Possibly “wealth” or “lust”; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

chapters.n: …God will gather all her former lovers and enemies against her and expose her shame publicly. The nations she trusted would be the ones to destroy her.

f.w: I will gather all thy lovers

chapters.n: She will be judged under the law as an adulteress and murderer—both crimes carried the death penalty.

f.w: women that break wedlock and shed blood

chapters.n: Her shrines will be torn down, and she will be stripped of the finery God gave her, left as she was at the beginning.
A crowd will stone her and cut her down—the legal punishment for adultery and idolatry, here carried out by invading armies.

f.w: they shall stone thee with stones

chapters.n: Her houses will be burned before the watching nations. Then her unfaithfulness will end.

f.w: they shall burn thine houses with fire

chapters.n: Then God’s fury will rest; his jealousy will turn away, and he will be calm. Judgment has a limit.

f.w: my jealousy shall depart from thee

chapters.n: Because she forgot her youth and provoked God, he will bring her conduct back on her own head.

f.g: Provoked or enraged me.

chapters.n: A proverb: “Like mother, like daughter.” Jerusalem has become just like the pagan peoples she came from.

f.w: As is the mother, so is her daughter
f.g: The second section of the chapter compares Jerusalem to her “sisters.”

chapters.n: Like her pagan “mother” and “sisters,” she despised her husband and children.

f.w: that lotheth her husband and her children
f.g: Who rejected her covenant God and sacrificed her children.

chapters.n: Her “older sister” is Samaria, the fallen northern kingdom to the north; her “younger sister” is Sodom to the south. (Facing east, left is north and right is south.)

f.g: Capital of the northern kingdom, destroyed by Assyria in 722 BC.

chapters.n: Jerusalem didn’t merely copy them; she quickly became even more corrupt.

f.w: as if that were a very little thing
f.g: As if their sins were too small for her.

chapters.n: God swears that Sodom never did as much evil as Jerusalem has. Greater knowledge makes sin more serious.

f.w: Sodom thy sister hath not done

chapters.n: Sodom’s sins included pride, overabundance, careless ease, and refusing to help the poor and needy. This verse shows that neglecting the poor was among the roots of Sodom’s destruction.

f.w: pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness

chapters.n: They were arrogant and did detestable things before God, so he removed them.
Samaria didn’t commit half Jerusalem’s sins. By comparison, Jerusalem makes her sisters look righteous.

f.g: Made them seem righteous in comparison.

chapters.n: Jerusalem, who once looked down on her sisters, must now bear her own shame. Judging others while sinning ourselves is a dangerous blindness.

f.g: Put to shame.

chapters.n: A surprising promise: God will restore the fortunes of Sodom and Samaria—and of Jerusalem along with them.

f.w: When I shall bring again their captivity
f.g: Restore their fortunes.

chapters.n: Being restored alongside those she despised will humble Jerusalem; it will comfort her sisters to see that she was no better.

f.w: in that thou art a comfort unto them
f.g: Her greater sin makes them feel less judged.

chapters.n: All three sisters will return to their former state. The promise points to a restoration bigger than Israel alone.
In her proud days Jerusalem used Sodom as a byword of wickedness, never thinking of her own sins.

f.w: was not mentioned by thy mouth
f.g: Or “was a byword in your mouth.”

chapters.n: That was before her own wickedness was exposed—now she is mocked by Syria, the Philistines, and her neighbors.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “Edom,” which differs from “Aram” (Syria) by one similar Hebrew letter.

chapters.n: Jerusalem must bear the consequences of her lewdness and abominations.

f.g: You are bearing the results.

chapters.n: God will deal with her as she dealt with him: she treated her covenant oath with contempt and broke it.

f.w: despised the oath in breaking the covenant

chapters.n: The great turn: “Nevertheless.” God will remember the covenant he made with her in her youth and establish an everlasting covenant. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the restored new and everlasting covenant.
Remembering her ways, she will be ashamed. She will receive her “sisters” as daughters—not because they were part of the old covenant, but through God’s new grace.

f.g: Not because of Jerusalem’s own faithfulness, but by God’s gift.

chapters.n: God will establish his covenant, and she will know he is the LORD.

f.w: I will establish my covenant with thee

chapters.n: When God forgives her completely, she will be humbled into silence. Forgiveness does not make sin trivial; it leads to deep gratitude and humility.

f.w: when I am pacified toward thee
f.g: When I have made atonement for you (Hebrew kipper).

chapters.n: A new message comes in the form of a riddle—an allegory about eagles, a cedar, and a vine.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Ezekiel is to pose a riddle and tell a parable. Its meaning is explained in verses 11–21.

f.g: Hebrew ḥidah—a puzzling saying that needs interpretation.

chapters.n: A magnificent eagle (Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon) comes to Lebanon and takes the top of a cedar. The cedar represents the royal house of David in Jerusalem.

f.g: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon (v. 12).
Famous for cedars; here symbolizing Jerusalem, whose palace was built of Lebanese cedar.

chapters.n: He snaps off the topmost shoot—King Jehoiachin—and carries it to a land of trade, a city of merchants: Babylon.

f.g: A land of trade—Babylon (literally “the land of Canaan,” here meaning “merchant land”).

chapters.n: He takes a native seedling—Zedekiah, a member of the royal family—and plants it in fertile soil by abundant water.

f.g: A native Judean prince, Zedekiah.

chapters.n: It grows into a low, spreading vine whose branches turn toward the eagle—a lesser kingdom loyal to Babylon.

f.w: a spreading vine of low stature
f.g: Judah as a humble vassal state, not a towering cedar.

chapters.n: A second great eagle appears—Pharaoh of Egypt—and the vine bends its roots and branches toward him for water. Zedekiah turned to Egypt for help against Babylon.

f.g: Pharaoh Hophra (Apries) of Egypt.

chapters.n: Yet the vine had already been planted in good soil with plenty of water. It had everything it needed to flourish where it was.

f.w: planted in a good soil by great waters
f.g: Under Babylon’s rule Judah could have survived peacefully.

chapters.n: Will it thrive? No—it will be uprooted and its fruit stripped, and it will wither, easily pulled up.

f.w: shall he not pull up the roots thereof
f.g: Babylon will uproot the disloyal vine.

chapters.n: When the hot east wind blows, it will dry up right where it grew. The east wind symbolizes Babylon.

f.g: A scorching desert wind; an image of destruction from the east.

chapters.n: God now explains the riddle.

f.w: Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: The interpretation follows.

chapters.n: Don’t you understand? The king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and took its king and nobles to Babylon in 597 BC.
He made a covenant with a member of the royal family (Zedekiah) and put him under oath, taking away the nation’s strongest men.

f.w: hath taken an oath of him
f.g: Zedekiah swore loyalty in God’s name.

chapters.n: Babylon intended Judah to be a humble kingdom that would survive by keeping that treaty.

f.g: Lowly, humble.

chapters.n: But Zedekiah rebelled, sending envoys to Egypt for horses and troops. Can someone break a sworn covenant and escape?
God swears that Zedekiah will die in Babylon, the land of the king whose oath he despised. This was fulfilled.

f.w: in the midst of Babylon he shall die

chapters.n: Pharaoh’s great army will be of no help when Babylon builds siege works against Jerusalem.

f.w: Neither shall Pharaoh with his mighty army

chapters.n: Because Zedekiah gave his hand in pledge and then broke the oath, he will not escape. Promises matter to God, even ones made to pagans.

f.g: Shaken hands in a binding pledge.

chapters.n: The oath was sworn in the Lord’s name, so God calls it “mine oath” and “my covenant.” Breaking it was breaking faith with God himself.

f.w: mine oath that he hath despised

chapters.n: God will catch Zedekiah in his net and bring him to Babylon to be judged for this betrayal.

f.w: I will spread my net upon him

f.g: Enter into judgment with him.

chapters.n: His fleeing troops will fall by the sword and the rest will be scattered—exactly as happened in 586 BC.

A messianic promise follows: God himself will take a tender shoot from the top of the cedar—David’s line—and plant it on a high mountain. Latter-day Saint readers have also noted the parallel with Mulek, a young son of Zedekiah whom the Lord led to the Americas.

f.w: I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar

chapters.n: Planted on Israel’s high mountain, it will become a majestic cedar sheltering birds of every kind—a picture of the Messiah’s kingdom welcoming all peoples. Jesus used similar imagery for the kingdom of God.

f.w: the mountain of the height of Israel
under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing

chapters.n: All nations will see that God brings down the proud and lifts up the humble, withers the green and makes the dry flourish. What God says, he does.

f.w: have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree

chapters.n: Another message. Chapter 18 is one of the clearest teachings in scripture on personal responsibility and repentance.

f.w: The word of the LORD came unto me again

chapters.n: People were quoting a proverb: “The parents ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are on edge.” In other words, “We’re being punished for our ancestors’ sins—it isn’t our fault.”

f.w: The fathers have eaten sour grapes

f.g: Made dull or sensitive, as when eating something sour.

chapters.n: God swears this excuse will no longer be used in Israel.
Every soul belongs to God—parent and child alike—and each person answers for his own sins. The Second Article of Faith expresses a similar principle.

f.w: the soul that sinneth, it shall die

chapters.n: Ezekiel gives a case study across three generations. First, a righteous man who does what is just and right…

f.g: Righteous, upright.

chapters.n: …who doesn’t feast at mountain idol shrines, worship idols, commit adultery, or break the purity laws of marriage…

f.g: Taken part in sacrificial meals at hilltop idol shrines.

chapters.n: …who doesn’t exploit others, returns a poor borrower’s pledge, never robs, feeds the hungry, and clothes the naked…

f.w: restored to the debtor his pledge
f.g: Returned the cloak or tool taken as collateral, so the poor were not left without necessities.

f.w: hath given his bread to the hungry

chapters.n: …who doesn’t charge interest to the needy, avoids wrongdoing, and judges fairly between people…

f.g: Interest on loans; Israelites were forbidden to charge it to fellow Israelites in need.
Profit or interest taken on a loan.

chapters.n: …and who follows God’s laws faithfully. Such a person is righteous and will surely live.
Second generation: suppose that righteous man has a son who becomes violent and bloodthirsty…

f.w: a robber, a shedder of blood
f.g: A violent man.

chapters.n: …who does none of his father’s good deeds but joins idol feasts and commits adultery…
…who oppresses the poor, robs, keeps pledges, and worships idols…
…and lends at interest. Will he live because his father was righteous? No. His blood is on his own head.

f.w: his blood shall be upon him
f.g: He alone is responsible for his death.

chapters.n: Third generation: suppose this wicked man has a son who sees his father’s sins, thinks it over, and chooses differently…

f.g: Reflects carefully—the first step toward a different life.

chapters.n: …who avoids idols and adultery…

f.w: lifted up his eyes to the idols
f.g: Looked to idols for help or worship.

chapters.n: …who oppresses no one, returns pledges, never robs, and feeds and clothes the needy…

f.w: hath covered the naked with a garment

chapters.n: …and keeps God’s laws. He will not die for his father’s sins; he will surely live. No one is trapped by their family’s past.

f.w: he shall not die for the iniquity of his father

chapters.n: His father, however, will die for his own oppression and violence.

f.g: Robbed his fellow Israelite.

chapters.n: The people object: “Why shouldn’t the son bear his father’s guilt?” God’s answer is firm: if the son does right, he will live.

f.w: doth not the son bear the iniquity of the father?

chapters.n: The principle stated plainly: each person bears his own righteousness or wickedness. Consequences can pass between generations, but guilt does not.

f.w: The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father

chapters.n: Even better news: if a wicked person turns from all his sins and does what is right, he will surely live.

f.w: if the wicked will turn from all his sins

chapters.n: His past sins will not be held against him; he will live because of the righteousness he now chooses. God truly forgives.

f.w: they shall not be mentioned unto him

chapters.n: One of the most tender verses in the Old Testament: God takes no pleasure in anyone’s death; he wants the wicked to turn and live.

f.w: Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die?

chapters.n: The reverse is also true: if a righteous person turns to wickedness and stays there, his former goodness won’t save him. Enduring to the end matters.

f.w: when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness

chapters.n: People complain, “The Lord’s way isn’t fair!” God answers: “Is it my way that is unfair—or yours?”

f.w: The way of the Lord is not equal
f.g: “Equal” here means fair or just.

chapters.n: A righteous person who turns to sin and dies in it dies for the sin he committed.

f.g: Dies without having repented.

chapters.n: A wicked person who turns from wickedness and does right saves his life.

f.w: he shall save his soul alive

chapters.n: Because he thoughtfully turns from all his transgressions, he will live. Repentance begins with reflection.
Still Israel says God is unfair. God repeats his challenge: it is your ways that are crooked.

f.g: Isn’t it your ways that are unjust?

chapters.n: God will judge each person by his own ways. So repent and turn, so that sin won’t be your downfall.

f.w: every one according to his ways
Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions

chapters.n: Throw away your sins and “make you a new heart and a new spirit.” In 11:19 and 36:26 God gives the new heart; here Israel must also act. Repentance is both God’s gift and our choice. “Why will you die?”

f.w: make you a new heart and a new spirit

chapters.n: The chapter ends with God’s heart laid bare: he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death. “Turn yourselves, and live.”
Ezekiel is told to sing a funeral lament (a qinah) for Israel’s “princes”—the last kings of Judah. It is written in the limping rhythm of Hebrew funeral songs.

f.g: Hebrew qinah, a dirge with a distinctive 3+2 beat rhythm.
Ezekiel’s usual term for Judah’s kings.

chapters.n: The “mother” is Judah (or the royal house), pictured as a lioness raising cubs among lions. The lion was Judah’s ancient emblem.

f.g: Cubs.

chapters.n: One cub grows into a young lion that learns to hunt and devours people—King Jehoahaz, who reigned only three months and did evil.

f.g: Jehoahaz, son of Josiah.

chapters.n: The nations trapped him and dragged him in hooks to Egypt. Pharaoh Necho deposed Jehoahaz and took him to Egypt, where he died.

f.w: they brought him with chains unto the land of Egypt
f.g: Literally “with hooks,” as captured animals were led.

chapters.n: When her hope was gone, the lioness raised another cub to be a young lion—most likely Jehoiachin (or possibly Zedekiah).

f.g: Probably Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC; some suggest Zedekiah.

chapters.n: He prowled among the lions, learned to hunt, and devoured people—another king who ruled by violence rather than justice.
He destroyed strongholds and ravaged cities; the land was terrified by his roaring.

f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; probably “he ravaged their strongholds.”

chapters.n: The surrounding nations set a net and caught him in their pit.
Caged and chained, he was brought to the king of Babylon so his roar would no longer be heard on Israel’s mountains.

f.w: brought him to the king of Babylon

f.g: A cage or prison.

chapters.n: The image changes: the mother is now a vine planted by plentiful water, fruitful and full of branches—Judah in its prosperous days.

f.w: like a vine in thy blood
