f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; perhaps “a vine in your vineyard.”

chapters.n: Her strong branches became royal scepters, and she stood tall among the clouds—the Davidic dynasty at its height.

f.w: strong rods for the sceptres of them that bare rule
f.g: Kings came from her branches.

chapters.n: But she was ripped up in anger and thrown down. The east wind dried her fruit, and fire burned her strongest branches.

f.w: the east wind dried up her fruit

chapters.n: Now she is replanted in a dry, thirsty desert—Judah in exile in Babylon.
Fire spread from one of her own branches—Zedekiah’s rebellion—and consumed her, leaving no strong branch to rule. “This is a lament, and has become a lament”: the prophecy was turning into history.

f.w: fire is gone out of a rod of her branches
f.g: The destruction came from within the royal family itself.

f.w: she hath no strong rod to be a sceptre to rule

chapters.n: About August 591 BC, elders again come to Ezekiel to ask the Lord a question. God responds with a review of Israel’s whole history of rebellion.

f.w: the seventh year, in the fifth month
f.g: About August 591 BC, counting from Jehoiachin’s exile.

f.w: came to inquire of the LORD

chapters.n: The Lord speaks to Ezekiel.

f.w: Then came the word of the LORD unto me
f.g: God answers the elders’ visit.

chapters.n: God refuses to be consulted by them. As in chapter 14, people still clinging to idols are not in a position to receive revelation.

f.w: I will not be inquired of by you

chapters.n: Instead of an oracle, Ezekiel is to “judge” them—confront them with the sins of their ancestors.

f.g: Bring an indictment against them.

chapters.n: It began in Egypt: God chose Israel, swore an oath to them (raising his hand), and revealed himself: “I am the LORD your God.”

f.g: A gesture of swearing an oath.

chapters.n: He swore to bring them to a land he had scouted for them—flowing with milk and honey, the most beautiful of lands.

f.g: Searched out, scouted.

chapters.n: God commanded them to throw away the idols of Egypt they loved to look at.

f.g: Idols they found attractive.

chapters.n: But they rebelled and kept their Egyptian idols. God was ready to pour out his anger even in Egypt.

f.w: neither did they forsake the idols of Egypt
f.g: This detail is not recorded in Exodus but fits Israel’s later behavior (the golden calf).

chapters.n: Yet God acted “for his name’s sake”—to protect his reputation before the nations who saw him deliver Israel. This phrase is the refrain of the chapter.

f.w: I wrought for my name's sake

chapters.n: So he brought them out of Egypt into the wilderness.
He gave them laws that bring life to those who live by them.

f.w: which if a man do, he shall even live in them

chapters.n: He also gave them his Sabbaths as a sign that it is the Lord who makes them holy. Sabbath-keeping was a mark of covenant identity.

f.w: my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them

chapters.n: Israel rebelled in the wilderness too, despising God’s laws and profaning his Sabbaths. God considered destroying them there.

f.w: rebelled against me in the wilderness

chapters.n: Again he spared them for his name’s sake.

f.w: that it should not be polluted before the heathen
f.g: So that his name would not be dishonored among the nations.

chapters.n: Still, God swore that the rebellious generation would not enter the promised land.

f.w: that I would not bring them into the land

chapters.n: This was because their hearts kept going after idols.

f.w: their heart went after their idols

chapters.n: Even so, God looked on them with pity and did not wipe them out.
He warned their children in the wilderness not to follow their parents’ ways or their idols. Each generation gets a fresh chance, as in chapter 18.

f.w: Walk ye not in the statutes of your fathers

chapters.n: “I am the LORD your God; walk in my statutes.”
Keep my Sabbaths holy as a sign of our relationship.

f.g: Keep holy.

chapters.n: But the children also rebelled, and God again was ready to pour out his anger.
Once more he held back his hand for the sake of his name.

f.g: Restrained his judgment.

chapters.n: Even in the wilderness God warned through Moses that persistent rebellion would end in scattering among the nations.

f.w: I would scatter them among the heathen

chapters.n: That scattering was the consequence of rejecting his laws and longing for their fathers’ idols.

f.w: their eyes were after their fathers' idols
f.g: Their desires stayed fixed on idols.

chapters.n: A difficult verse: God “gave them” laws that were not good. It likely means he let them follow the destructive pagan customs they chose—handing them over to their own choices as judgment.

f.g: Probably the corrupt practices they adopted, which God allowed as a consequence.

chapters.n: He let them defile themselves through their offerings—even sacrificing their firstborn children in fire—so that the horror would bring them to recognize the Lord.

f.w: caused to pass through the fire all that openeth the womb
f.g: Child sacrifice to Molech, a perversion of the law that the firstborn belonged to God.

chapters.n: After entering the land, their ancestors blasphemed God by being unfaithful.

f.g: Insulted, dishonored.

chapters.n: Once in Canaan they offered sacrifices on every high hill and under every leafy tree—offerings that provoked God.

f.w: every high hill, and all the thick trees

f.g: Wine poured out as an offering.

chapters.n: A sarcastic wordplay: “What is this high place (bamah) you go (ba’im) to?” The name stuck—they still called such places “Bamah.”

f.g: Hebrew for “high place.” The pun mocks the shrines.

chapters.n: Now God turns to the present generation: are you defiling yourselves just like your fathers?

f.w: Are ye polluted after the manner of your fathers?
f.g: The history lesson is aimed at the elders in front of Ezekiel.

chapters.n: Since they still make their sons pass through fire and worship idols, God will not let them consult him.

f.w: I will not be inquired of by you

chapters.n: Some thought, “Let’s just be like the other nations and worship wood and stone.” God says that will never happen; he won’t let his people simply disappear into paganism.

f.w: We will be as the heathen

chapters.n: God swears he will rule over them with a mighty hand and outstretched arm—the same power he used to free them from Egypt.

f.w: with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm

chapters.n: He will gather them out of the nations where they are scattered. A new exodus is promised.

f.w: will gather you out of the countries

chapters.n: He will bring them into “the wilderness of the peoples” and there judge them face to face, as he did at Sinai.

f.g: The lands of exile, pictured as a new wilderness journey.

chapters.n: As he judged their ancestors in the wilderness of Egypt, so he will judge them.

f.w: Like as I pleaded with your fathers

chapters.n: Like a shepherd counting sheep as they pass under his staff, God will examine each person and bring them into the covenant bond.

f.g: Shepherds counted and inspected sheep as they passed under a rod.

chapters.n: He will separate out the rebels; they will not enter the land of Israel—just as the rebellious wilderness generation did not.

f.w: I will purge out from among you the rebels

chapters.n: With bitter irony God says: go ahead and serve your idols if you won’t listen—but stop profaning my holy name by mixing them with my worship.

f.w: pollute ye my holy name no more

chapters.n: On God’s holy mountain, all Israel will one day serve him, and he will accept their offerings again—a promise of restored temple worship.

f.g: Offerings.

chapters.n: When he gathers them, he will accept them as a pleasing offering and show his holiness through them before the nations.

f.w: I will be sanctified in you before the heathen

chapters.n: Brought back to the land promised to their fathers, they will know he is the Lord.

f.w: I lifted up mine hand to give it to your fathers

chapters.n: There they will remember their past and feel deep sorrow for it. True repentance often comes most fully after experiencing God’s mercy.
They will know the Lord when they see that he dealt with them for his name’s sake—graciously—rather than as their sins deserved.

f.w: not according to your wicked ways

chapters.n: A new short oracle begins. (In the Hebrew Bible, verses 45–49 begin chapter 21.)

f.w: Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: Hebrew Bibles number 20:45-49 as 21:1-5.

chapters.n: Ezekiel turns toward the south—Judah, which lay south of the route Babylon’s armies would take—and prophesies against its “forest.”

f.g: Three different Hebrew words for “south” are used here, perhaps hinting at Judah and the Negev.
Let your words flow, preach.

chapters.n: God will light an unquenchable fire that burns every tree, green and dry, from south to north. Chapter 21 shows the fire is Babylon’s sword.

f.w: every green tree in thee, and every dry tree

chapters.n: Everyone will see that the Lord kindled this fire, and it won’t be put out.
Ezekiel complains: people dismiss him as just “a teller of parables.” His vivid stories were being treated as entertainment rather than warning—so in chapter 21 God speaks plainly.
Now God explains the “parable” of the forest fire in plain terms. (Hebrew Bibles number this as 21:6.)

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Ezekiel faces Jerusalem, its sanctuaries, and the land of Israel. The “south forest” of chapter 20 is now named outright.

f.g: The temple and its courts.

chapters.n: God draws his sword against the land, cutting off both righteous and wicked. Invasion would sweep up everyone, though God still knows his own (9:4).

f.w: will draw forth my sword out of his sheath

f.g: In war, physical suffering falls on all, though eternal judgment remains individual.

chapters.n: Because both will be cut off, the sword will sweep the whole land from south to north—the “green and dry trees” of 20:47.

f.w: from the south to the north

chapters.n: Everyone will know the Lord drew this sword, and it will not be put back until its work is done.

f.w: it shall not return any more

chapters.n: Ezekiel must groan as if his body were breaking, bitterly and in public—another acted sign.

f.w: with the breaking of thy loins
f.g: With a groan that seems to come from his very core.

chapters.n: When people ask why he groans, he answers: “Because of the news that is coming.” Every heart will melt, hands go limp, and knees turn to water.

f.g: The news of Jerusalem’s fall (see 33:21).

chapters.n: A new message follows: “the Song of the Sword.”

f.w: Again the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: Verses 8–17 are a fierce poem.

chapters.n: “A sword, a sword, sharpened and polished!” The repetition builds dread.

f.g: Polished.

chapters.n: It is sharpened for slaughter and polished to flash like lightning. Should anyone celebrate? The sword scorns the royal scepter of Judah as if it were just another stick.

f.g: Is this a time for rejoicing? No.
Probably Judah’s royal scepter; the Hebrew is very difficult.

chapters.n: The sword is handed over polished and ready for the slayer—Nebuchadnezzar.

f.g: The executioner—Babylon’s king.

chapters.n: Cry and wail, Ezekiel, for the sword is aimed at God’s own people and their leaders. Slapping the thigh was a sign of grief.

f.g: A gesture of mourning and dismay.

chapters.n: It is a time of testing. What if even the scepter is rejected? It will be no more—Judah’s kingship will end.

f.w: what if the sword contemn even the rod?
f.g: The Hebrew is obscure; it seems to say the scepter itself will be despised and removed.

chapters.n: Ezekiel claps his hands as the sword strikes again and again—a sword for great slaughter that reaches even into private rooms.

f.w: let the sword be doubled the third time
f.g: Let it strike twice, three times—repeatedly.
Inner, private rooms.

chapters.n: The sword’s point is at every gate, so hearts fail and many fall. It flashes like lightning, drawn for slaughter.

f.w: it is wrapped up for the slaughter
f.g: Gripped, ready to strike.

chapters.n: The sword is addressed: slash to the right, to the left, wherever you are aimed.

f.g: In whatever direction you are pointed.

chapters.n: God himself claps his hands, and his anger will be satisfied.

f.w: I will cause my fury to rest

chapters.n: A new message with another acted-out sign.

f.w: The word of the LORD came unto me again
f.g: This oracle pictures Babylon’s king choosing his target.

chapters.n: Ezekiel draws a road map: two routes branching from one land, with a signpost at the fork pointing toward the cities.

f.g: Mark out two roads.
Literally “cut a hand”—a signpost.

chapters.n: One road leads to Rabbah, capital of Ammon (modern Amman, Jordan); the other to fortified Jerusalem. Both had rebelled against Babylon.

f.g: Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, today Amman, Jordan.

chapters.n: At the fork, Nebuchadnezzar seeks omens: shaking arrows, consulting household idols, and examining a sacrificed animal’s liver—common Babylonian methods of divination.

f.g: Belomancy—drawing marked arrows from a quiver like casting lots.
Hebrew teraphim, household idols.
Hepatoscopy—reading omens from an animal liver, a common Babylonian practice.

chapters.n: The omen in his right hand says “Jerusalem.” He orders commanders forward, battle cries, battering rams, siege ramps, and siege walls. God uses even a pagan king’s fortune-telling to accomplish his purpose.

f.w: to appoint battering rams against the gates

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s people will think the omen is false because of their treaty oaths. But the king will remember their rebellion, and they will be captured.

f.w: to them that have sworn oaths
f.g: Those who had sworn loyalty to Babylon and then broken it.

chapters.n: Because their sins are now out in the open for all to see, they will be taken captive.

f.w: ye shall be taken with the hand
f.g: Seized, captured.

chapters.n: Ezekiel addresses Zedekiah directly: “You profane, wicked prince of Israel, your day has come.”

f.g: King Zedekiah.

chapters.n: Remove the turban and take off the crown. Everything will be turned upside down: the lowly raised, the proud brought low.

f.g: A turban—possibly the high priest’s turban, suggesting both kingship and priesthood fail.

f.w: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high

chapters.n: “A ruin, a ruin, a ruin!” Judah’s kingship will cease until the one comes to whom it rightfully belongs. Christians understand this as pointing to Jesus Christ, the rightful heir of David’s throne.

f.w: I will overturn, overturn, overturn, it
f.g: The threefold repeat expresses total ruin.

f.w: until he come whose right it is

chapters.n: Ammon, which escaped this time, should not gloat. The sword is drawn for it too.

f.g: Their taunting of Israel.

chapters.n: Ammon’s own false visions and lies promised safety, but they too will fall with the slain.

f.w: Whiles they see vanity unto thee
f.g: While false seers give you empty hopes.

chapters.n: Put the sword back—Ammon will be judged in its own homeland.

f.w: in the land of thy nativity
f.g: In its own country.

chapters.n: God will pour out his anger on Ammon and hand it over to brutal men skilled at destruction.

f.g: Savage, cruel men.

chapters.n: Ammon will be fuel for the fire and be forgotten. Unlike Israel, it receives no promise of restoration here; Ammon as a nation later vanished from history.

f.w: thou shalt be no more remembered

chapters.n: A new message lists Jerusalem’s sins like a legal indictment.

f.w: Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Will you judge “the bloody city”? Show her all her detestable deeds. Nahum used the same title for Nineveh.
Jerusalem sheds blood and makes idols—sins against people and against God—hurrying her own day of judgment.

f.g: Bringing her day of reckoning closer.

chapters.n: Her guilt has shortened her days and made her a laughingstock among nations.

f.w: art come even unto thy years
f.g: You have reached the end of your time.

chapters.n: Nations near and far will mock her infamous name and her turmoil.

f.g: Notorious and full of chaos.

chapters.n: Her rulers each used their power to shed blood instead of protect.

f.g: As much as they could, by their power.

chapters.n: Parents are disrespected; foreigners, orphans, and widows—the most vulnerable—are exploited. The law specifically protected these groups.

f.w: set light by father and mother
vexed the fatherless and the widow

chapters.n: They scorn God’s holy things and profane his Sabbaths.
Slanderers spread lies to get people killed; others eat at idol shrines and commit immoral acts.

f.g: Slanderers and informers.

chapters.n: Sexual sins forbidden in the law—incest and violating a woman during her impurity—are committed openly.

f.g: Committed incest with a father’s wife.

f.w: her that was set apart for pollution
f.g: A woman during her monthly impurity.

chapters.n: Adultery, sins with a daughter-in-law, and incest with a half-sister—family boundaries are being destroyed.
Bribes for murder, interest on loans to the poor, and extortion. At the root of it all: “thou hast forgotten me.”
God strikes his hands together in anger at their dishonest profits and bloodshed.
When God acts, will their courage hold? He has spoken, and he will do it.
He will scatter them among the nations to burn away their uncleanness. Exile is meant to purify, not just punish.

f.w: will consume thy filthiness out of thee

chapters.n: Jerusalem will be profaned in the eyes of the nations, and then she will know the Lord.

f.w: thou shalt take thine inheritance in thyself
f.g: Probably “you will be profaned through yourself”; the Hebrew can be read either way.

chapters.n: Another message: the image of a refiner’s furnace.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Israel has become “dross”—the worthless metals left after silver is refined. They are copper, tin, iron, and lead, with no silver left.

f.g: Impurities skimmed off molten metal.

chapters.n: So God will gather them all into Jerusalem as into a furnace—the siege.

f.w: I will gather you into the midst of Jerusalem
f.g: Refugees fled into the city before the Babylonian siege.

chapters.n: As ore is gathered into a furnace and heated with bellows, God will gather them in his anger and melt them.

f.w: to blow the fire upon it
f.g: Using bellows to intensify the heat.

chapters.n: He will blow on them with the fire of his wrath until they melt.

f.w: blow upon you in the fire of my wrath

chapters.n: As silver melts in a furnace, so will they. Refining is painful, but it is how the precious is separated from the worthless.
Another message surveys every class of leaders.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: Verses 23–31 indict every group in society.

chapters.n: Judah is a land not cleansed by rain—spiritually dry and unwashed in the day of God’s anger.

f.g: Rain was a sign of God’s blessing; drought a sign of judgment.

chapters.n: Her prophets conspire like roaring lions tearing prey: they devour people, seize treasure, and leave many widows.

f.g: The Greek version reads “princes,” which fits the list well.

chapters.n: Her priests break God’s law and fail to teach the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean—their central duty.

f.w: they have put no difference between the holy and profane

chapters.n: Her officials are like wolves tearing prey, killing people for dishonest gain.
Her prophets whitewash these crimes with false visions, claiming “Thus saith the Lord” when he has not spoken.
Ordinary people too practice extortion and robbery, mistreating the poor, needy, and foreigners. Sin has spread through every level of society.

f.g: The landowning citizens.

chapters.n: God searched for one person to rebuild the wall and stand in the breach before him on behalf of the land, but found no one. Moses had once stood in such a gap; ultimately Christ is the great Intercessor.
So God has poured out his anger and brought their own conduct down upon their heads. Judgment is the harvest of their own choices.

f.w: their own way have I recompensed upon their heads

chapters.n: Chapter 23 is another blunt allegory, this time about two sisters. Like chapter 16, it uses the picture of marital unfaithfulness to show how deeply Israel’s idolatry and foreign alliances wounded her covenant with God.

f.w: The word of the LORD came again unto me

chapters.n: Two sisters, daughters of one mother, represent the two kingdoms that grew from one people, Israel.

f.w: two women, the daughters of one mother
f.g: Northern Israel and southern Judah, divided after Solomon.

chapters.n: Even in their youth in Egypt they were unfaithful—Israel adopted Egyptian idols before the Exodus.
Their names are Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem). Both belonged to God and bore him children—the people of each kingdom.

f.g: “Her tent”—perhaps implying Samaria had her own unauthorized shrines.
“My tent is in her”—God’s own sanctuary was in Jerusalem, making her betrayal worse.

chapters.n: Samaria, while still God’s, chased after her lovers, the Assyrians—seeking security through alliances rather than through God.
She was dazzled by Assyria’s impressive officers—uniformed, mounted, and powerful. Political glamour led her away.

f.g: Purple or blue garments, a sign of wealth and rank.

chapters.n: She gave herself to Assyria’s elite and defiled herself with their idols.

f.w: with all their idols she defiled herself

chapters.n: She never gave up the habits she began in Egypt.
So God handed her over to the very Assyrians she desired.

f.w: delivered her into the hand of her lovers

chapters.n: Assyria exposed and destroyed her, took her children captive, and killed her. Samaria became a byword among nations (722 BC).

f.g: Her fate became notorious.

chapters.n: Jerusalem saw what happened to her sister—yet became even more corrupt. Failing to learn from another’s example makes guilt greater.

f.w: she was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she

chapters.n: She too chased Assyria’s splendid officers—Judah’s King Ahaz famously asked Assyria for help.
God saw she was defiled and took the same path as her sister.

f.g: Both went the same way.

chapters.n: She went further: seeing pictures of Babylonian men painted in red on walls, she was attracted to Babylon as well.

f.g: A bright red pigment used in wall paintings.

chapters.n: These images showed Babylonian officers in fine belts and flowing headdresses—the look of an impressive empire.

f.g: Flowing, colorful turbans.

chapters.n: As soon as she saw them she was infatuated and sent messengers to Babylon. Judah’s kings did court Babylon’s favor.

f.w: sent messengers unto them into Chaldea

chapters.n: The Babylonians came, defiled her, and then she grew disgusted with them—Judah later rebelled against Babylon.

f.w: her mind was alienated from them
f.g: She turned away from them in disgust.

chapters.n: Her shamelessness was public, and God turned away from her as he had from her sister.

f.w: my mind was alienated from her

chapters.n: Yet she went back to Egypt, remembering her youth—Zedekiah turned to Egypt for help against Babylon.

f.w: in calling to remembrance the days of her youth

chapters.n: She lusted after Egypt with crude, animal-like desire. Ezekiel’s coarse imagery is meant to shock readers into seeing how degrading their trust in Egypt was.

f.g: Lovers; here Egypt’s rulers.

chapters.n: She longed again for the corruption of her youth in Egypt.

f.g: Israel’s idolatry dating back to Egypt.

chapters.n: Now God will raise up those very lovers—the Babylonians she had grown disgusted with—against her from every side.

f.w: I will raise up thy lovers against thee

chapters.n: Babylon and its allies—Chaldeans, Pekod, Shoa, Koa, and Assyrians—will come, impressive horsemen all.

f.g: Peoples east of the Tigris within the Babylonian empire; Pekod is known from Babylonian records.

chapters.n: They will come with chariots, wagons, and shields. God will let them judge her by their own harsh standards.

f.g: A large shield.

f.w: they shall judge thee according to their judgments
f.g: By their own brutal customs.

chapters.n: God’s jealous love, betrayed, will allow them to treat her with fury. Mutilation was a known punishment in the ancient Near East; here it pictures the brutal treatment of captives.

f.w: they shall take away thy nose and thine ears
f.g: A punishment practiced in Assyria and Egypt.

chapters.n: They will strip her of her clothing and fine jewelry.
Thus God will end her unfaithfulness and her longing for Egypt.

f.g: She will finally stop looking to Egypt for help.

chapters.n: God will hand her to those she now hates.

f.g: The Babylonians.

chapters.n: They will treat her with hatred, take everything she worked for, and leave her bare and exposed.

f.g: Seize the fruit of her work.

chapters.n: This happens because she chased the nations and defiled herself with their idols.
She walked in her sister’s path, so she will drink her sister’s cup.

f.g: A cup of judgment.

chapters.n: The cup is deep and wide—full of mockery and scorn.

f.g: Ridiculed.

chapters.n: She will be filled with drunken misery: the cup of horror and ruin—Samaria’s cup.

f.w: the cup of astonishment and desolation

chapters.n: She will drain it, gnaw its broken pieces, and tear at herself in despair.

f.g: Broken pottery fragments.

chapters.n: The root sin: “Because you have forgotten me and thrown me behind your back.” God was treated as something to discard.
God asks Ezekiel to judge both sisters and declare their detestable acts.

f.w: wilt thou judge Aholah and Aholibah?

chapters.n: Their crimes: idolatry pictured as adultery, bloodshed, and sacrificing the children they bore to God.

f.w: to pass for them through the fire

chapters.n: On the very same day, they defiled God’s temple and profaned his Sabbaths.

f.g: Mixing pagan worship and temple worship without shame.

chapters.n: After killing their children for idols, they walked straight into God’s temple—worshipping him with blood on their hands.

f.w: then they came the same day into my sanctuary

chapters.n: They sent for foreign envoys and prepared for them like a woman beautifying herself—bathing, painting her eyes, and wearing jewelry.

f.g: Applied eye makeup, as Jezebel did.

chapters.n: She reclined on a fine couch at a banquet table and set out God’s own incense and oil for her guests.
A carefree crowd surrounded her, including drunkards brought from the desert, who adorned the sisters with bracelets and crowns.

f.g: Probably “drunkards” (a similar Hebrew word); either way, rough desert visitors.

chapters.n: God remarks: even this worn-out adulteress still goes on with her unfaithfulness.

f.w: her that was old in adulteries
f.g: One worn out by long unfaithfulness.

chapters.n: Yet they kept coming to both sisters.

f.g: The two unfaithful sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Righteous judges will sentence them as adulteresses and murderers, because that is what they are.

f.w: the righteous men, they shall judge them
f.g: Even the nations used as God’s instruments act “righteously” in carrying out his sentence here.

chapters.n: God will bring an army against them to terrorize and plunder.

f.g: To be tossed about and looted.

chapters.n: The army will stone them, cut them down, kill their children, and burn their houses—the legal penalties for adultery and idolatry, carried out in war.
This will end such unfaithfulness in the land and serve as a warning to all.

f.w: that all women may be taught
f.g: That all may learn from their example.

chapters.n: They will bear the consequences of their idolatry—and in that they will come to know the Lord GOD.

f.w: ye shall bear the sins of your idols

chapters.n: A dated message: the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year—about January 588 BC. This very day the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem began, hundreds of miles away.

f.w: in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth day

chapters.n: Ezekiel must write the date down. When news later arrives, the exiles will know God revealed it to him on the exact day. Jews still fast on the tenth of Tevet to remember it.

f.w: write thee the name of the day
f.g: Record the date as evidence of true prophecy.

chapters.n: Another parable for the rebellious house: put a pot on the fire and pour in water. This recalls the leaders’ boast that Jerusalem was a safe “caldron” (11:3).
Fill it with the best cuts—thigh and shoulder—and choice bones. These represent Jerusalem’s leading citizens.

f.g: The choicest meat—the city’s elite.

chapters.n: Use the best of the flock, pile wood underneath, and boil it hard until even the bones are cooked—the siege will be intense.

f.g: Boil.

chapters.n: Woe to the bloody city, a pot crusted with rust (“scum”) that won’t come off. Empty it piece by piece without casting lots—no one will be chosen to be spared.

f.g: Probably rust or corrosion—a picture of deep-set guilt.

f.w: let no lot fall upon it
f.g: No selection; all will be removed.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s bloodshed is exposed on bare rock, not covered with dust as the law required for spilled blood. Her violence is open and unashamed.
So God has left her blood uncovered, crying out for justice.

f.w: that it should not be covered

chapters.n: Woe to the bloody city! God himself will build the woodpile high.
Pile on wood, light the fire, cook the meat well, and let the bones burn. Judgment will be thorough.

f.g: Possibly “boil it down” or “mix in spices.”

chapters.n: Then set the empty pot on the coals until the bronze glows hot and the rust burns away. Even purging the city itself becomes necessary.

f.w: that the filthiness of it may be molten in it

chapters.n: All the effort has failed; her heavy rust won’t come off. It must go into the fire.

f.w: She hath wearied herself with lies
f.g: Or “it has wearied all efforts”—the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: God tried to cleanse her through earlier warnings, but she refused to be cleansed. Now she won’t be clean until his anger is spent.

f.w: because I have purged thee, and thou wast not purged

chapters.n: God has spoken and will act; he won’t turn back or relent. Their own deeds will be their judges.

f.g: Neither will I change my mind.

chapters.n: Another message—one of the most personal moments in all the prophets.

f.w: Also the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: The following sign costs Ezekiel deeply.

chapters.n: God tells Ezekiel he is about to take away “the desire of his eyes”—his beloved wife—suddenly. Yet he must not mourn publicly or weep.

f.g: The one he loved most—his wife (v. 18).
Suddenly, by a single blow.

chapters.n: He may groan silently but must not perform the customary mourning rites: he keeps his turban and sandals on, doesn’t cover his face, and doesn’t eat the meal neighbors bring to mourners.

f.w: bind the tire of thine head upon thee
f.g: Keep your turban on, rather than baring your head in grief.
Covering the lower face was a sign of mourning.
The meal friends brought to a grieving family.

chapters.n: Ezekiel spoke to the people in the morning; that evening his wife died. The next morning he obeyed. His quiet obedience in deep grief is one of the most moving moments in the book.

f.g: The only mention of Ezekiel’s wife.

f.w: I did in the morning as I was commanded

chapters.n: Puzzled that he isn’t mourning, the people ask what it means for them.
Ezekiel explains God’s message.

f.w: The word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: His silence was a message from God.

chapters.n: God will profane his sanctuary—the temple that is Israel’s pride, the delight of their eyes, the object of their deepest longing. Their children left in Jerusalem will die by the sword.

f.g: The same phrase used for Ezekiel’s wife (v. 16).

chapters.n: When the news comes, they will react as Ezekiel did—without the usual mourning rituals.

f.w: ye shall do as I have done
f.g: Their loss will be too overwhelming for normal mourning.

chapters.n: They will not weep openly but will waste away because of their sins and groan to one another. Shock and guilt will leave them numb.

f.w: ye shall pine away for your iniquities

chapters.n: Ezekiel himself is the sign. When it happens, they will know the Lord. This is the only place the prophet’s name appears outside chapter 1.

f.w: Ezekiel is unto you a sign

chapters.n: On the day God takes away their stronghold, their joy and glory, the delight of their eyes, and their children…

f.w: that whereupon they set their minds
f.g: What they longed for most.

chapters.n: …a survivor will escape and bring the news to Ezekiel.
On that day Ezekiel’s silence will end; he will speak freely again. The fulfillment comes in 33:21–22, when a refugee reports “The city is fallen.”
Chapters 25–32 turn to oracles against foreign nations. Placed between Jerusalem’s siege (ch. 24) and news of its fall (ch. 33), they show that God judges all nations, not only Israel.

f.w: The word of the LORD came again unto me

chapters.n: First, Ammon, east of the Jordan—descendants of Lot.

f.g: Descendants of Lot, living east of the Jordan around Rabbah.

chapters.n: Ammon cheered “Aha!” when the temple was profaned, the land ruined, and Judah exiled. Gloating over others’ suffering is itself a sin.

f.g: A taunting shout of glee.

chapters.n: So God will give Ammon to desert tribes from the east, who will camp there and eat its produce.

f.g: Nomadic tribes from the Arabian desert.

chapters.n: Rabbah, Ammon’s capital, will become a pasture for camels and sheep.
Ammon clapped and stamped with delight, full of contempt for Israel.

f.g: Spite, malice.

chapters.n: God will hand Ammon over to plunder and wipe it out as a nation.

f.w: I will cause thee to perish out of the countries

chapters.n: Next Moab and Seir (Edom) said Judah was just like every other nation—denying that Israel’s God and covenant were special.

f.g: Descendants of Lot, east of the Dead Sea.
Mocking Israel’s claim to be God’s chosen people.

chapters.n: God will expose Moab’s flank by opening its border towns—its glory—to invaders.

f.g: Towns on Moab’s northwestern plateau.

chapters.n: Moab, like Ammon, will be given to the eastern tribes, and Ammon will be forgotten.

f.w: that the Ammonites may not be remembered

chapters.n: God will judge Moab, and it will know he is the Lord.

f.w: I will execute judgments upon Moab

chapters.n: Edom—Esau’s descendants—took revenge on Judah when it fell, an act that Obadiah and the Psalms remember bitterly.

f.g: Descendants of Esau, south of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: God will lay Edom waste from Teman in the north to Dedan in the south.

f.g: A leading Edomite region.
An Arabian oasis southeast of Edom.

chapters.n: Strikingly, God will use Israel itself as his instrument against Edom. Later, the Hasmonean Jewish rulers did conquer the Edomites (Idumeans).

f.w: by the hand of my people Israel

chapters.n: The Philistines, Israel’s ancient coastal enemies, acted with spiteful revenge rooted in “old hatred.”

f.g: Centuries of hostility going back to the judges and Saul.

chapters.n: God will cut off the Cherethites and the rest of the coastal peoples.

f.g: Cherethites, a group linked with the Philistines and possibly from Crete.

chapters.n: God will take great vengeance on them, and they will know he is the Lord. The nations’ hatred will not have the final word over God’s people.

f.w: they shall know that I am the LORD

chapters.n: Dated to the eleventh year (about 587–586 BC), around Jerusalem’s fall, this begins three chapters about Tyre, the wealthy Phoenician trading city on the coast of modern Lebanon.

f.g: About 587/586 BC; the month is not given in the Hebrew.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Tyre rejoiced: “Aha! Jerusalem, the gateway of the nations, is broken. Now her trade will come to me.” Tyre saw Judah’s disaster as a business opportunity.

f.g: Tyre, a Phoenician port partly on an island just off the coast; famous for sea trade and purple dye.
Jerusalem controlled inland trade routes.

chapters.n: God is against Tyre and will send nation after nation against her like waves crashing on her island.

f.w: as the sea causeth his waves to come up
f.g: A fitting image for an island city—many waves over a long time.

chapters.n: Her walls and towers will fall; God will scrape her down to bare rock—a play on Tyre’s name, which means “rock.”

f.g: Tyre (Hebrew Tsor) means “rock.”

chapters.n: She will become a place where fishermen spread their nets to dry—a striking image of a once-busy port reduced to nothing.

f.w: a place for the spreading of nets

chapters.n: Her “daughters”—towns on the mainland—will be put to the sword.

f.w: her daughters which are in the field
f.g: Tyre’s dependent settlements on the mainland.

chapters.n: God names the first wave: Nebuchadnezzar, “king of kings,” coming from the north with a great army.

f.g: A spelling closer to the Babylonian Nabû-kudurri-uṣur.
A title used by Mesopotamian emperors.

chapters.n: He will destroy the mainland towns and build siege works against Tyre.
Battering rams will strike her walls, and axes will cut down her towers.

f.g: Battering rams.

chapters.n: His horses will raise clouds of dust, and the walls will shake as his chariots thunder through breached gates.

f.g: A gap broken in a city wall.

chapters.n: He will trample her streets, kill her people, and topple her mighty pillars.

f.g: Probably her sacred pillars—Tyre’s temples had famous pillars.

chapters.n: Note the shift to “they”: enemies will loot Tyre’s wealth and throw her stones, timber, and rubble into the sea. Alexander the Great did exactly this in 332 BC, using the ruins of mainland Tyre to build a causeway to the island.

f.w: they shall lay thy stones and thy timber and thy dust in the midst of the water
f.g: Fulfilled strikingly in Alexander’s siege of 332 BC.

chapters.n: Tyre’s songs and harps—the sounds of a prosperous party city—will fall silent.

f.w: the sound of thy harps shall be no more heard

chapters.n: She will be bare rock for drying nets and never rebuilt as she was. Old Tyre’s glory never returned, though a later town grew nearby.

f.w: thou shalt be built no more
f.g: The great city-state never regained its former power.

chapters.n: Coastal lands will shake at the noise of her fall.

f.g: Coastlands and islands of the Mediterranean that traded with Tyre.

chapters.n: The sea-kings will step down from their thrones, remove their royal robes, and sit trembling on the ground in mourning.

f.g: Rulers of other trading cities.

f.w: they shall clothe themselves with trembling

chapters.n: They will lament: “How you are destroyed, famous city of sailors, once mighty on the sea and feared by all!”

f.g: A funeral lament formula.

chapters.n: The coastlands will tremble at her collapse.

f.g: Your end.

chapters.n: God will make Tyre an empty ruin, covered by the ocean depths.

f.w: bring up the deep upon thee
f.g: The primeval deep, a symbol of chaos and death.

chapters.n: He will send her down to the pit—the realm of the dead—with ancient peoples, while he gives glory to the land of the living (Israel).

f.g: The grave or underworld (Sheol).

f.w: I shall set glory in the land of the living
f.g: Possibly “you will no longer have a place in the land of the living.”

chapters.n: Tyre will come to a terrifying end; people will search for her, but she will never be found again as she was.

f.w: yet shalt thou never be found again

chapters.n: Another message: a lament for Tyre, pictured as a magnificent merchant ship. Revelation 18 later echoes this chapter in its lament for “Babylon.”

f.w: The word of the LORD came again unto me

chapters.n: Ezekiel is to sing a funeral song for Tyre—while she is still thriving.
Tyre sits at the gateway to the sea, trading with many coastlands. She boasts, “I am perfect in beauty.” Pride is the core of her sin.
Her territory is the sea, and her builders made her beautiful—a perfect ship.

f.w: Thy borders are in the midst of the seas
f.g: Tyre’s island setting made her like a ship anchored offshore.

chapters.n: Her planks came from fir (juniper) trees of Mount Hermon and her mast from a cedar of Lebanon.

f.g: The Amorite name for Mount Hermon.

chapters.n: Her oars were of Bashan oak; her deck was cypress inlaid with ivory from Cyprus.

f.g: A fertile region east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for oaks.
Kittim—Cyprus and the western coastlands.

chapters.n: Her sail was embroidered Egyptian linen; her awnings were blue and purple from Elishah (likely Cyprus).

f.g: Probably Alashiya, an ancient name for Cyprus.

chapters.n: Men of Sidon and Arvad, neighboring Phoenician cities, were her rowers; Tyre’s own experts were her captains.

f.g: Sidon and Arvad, Phoenician ports north of Tyre.

chapters.n: Veteran craftsmen of Gebal (Byblos) sealed her seams, and sailors from every ship came to trade with her.

f.g: Byblos, an ancient Phoenician city known for shipbuilding.
Workers who sealed a ship’s seams against leaks.

chapters.n: Mercenaries from Persia, Lud, and Put served in her army, hanging their shields on her walls as decoration.

f.w: Persia and of Lud and of Phut
f.g: Persia, Lydia (in Asia Minor), and Put (Libya)—soldiers hired from distant lands.

chapters.n: Men of Arvad and Gammad guarded her walls and towers, their shields adding to her splendor.

f.g: An unknown people—perhaps “valorous men.”

chapters.n: Verses 12–24 list Tyre’s trading partners like a ship’s cargo manifest. Tarshish, far to the west (possibly Spain), traded silver, iron, tin, and lead.

f.g: A distant western port, often identified with Tartessus in Spain.

chapters.n: Greece (Javan), Tubal, and Meshech in Asia Minor traded slaves and bronze vessels.

f.g: Ionian Greeks and peoples of Anatolia.
Slaves—condemned elsewhere in scripture.

chapters.n: Beth-togarmah (in Armenia) supplied horses, war horses, and mules.

f.g: A region in eastern Anatolia/Armenia.

chapters.n: Dedan and many coastlands brought ivory tusks and ebony as payment.

f.g: Elephant tusks and black hardwood from Africa or India.

chapters.n: Aram (Syria)—or perhaps Edom—traded gems, purple fabric, embroidery, linen, coral, and rubies.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “Edom.”
Possibly ruby.

chapters.n: Judah and Israel supplied agricultural goods: wheat, millet (or pastries), honey, oil, and balm.

f.g: An Ammonite town.
Unknown; perhaps a kind of cake or millet.

chapters.n: Damascus traded wine from Helbon and white wool.

f.g: A region north of Damascus famous for wine.

chapters.n: Others brought wrought iron and spices like cassia and calamus.

f.g: Fragrant spices used in perfumes and holy anointing oil.

chapters.n: Dedan supplied saddle blankets for riding.

f.g: Saddlecloths.

chapters.n: Arabia and the princes of Kedar traded lambs, rams, and goats.

f.g: A powerful Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael.

chapters.n: Sheba and Raamah in southern Arabia brought the finest spices, precious stones, and gold.

f.g: A wealthy kingdom in southwest Arabia (modern Yemen).

chapters.n: Mesopotamian cities—Haran, Canneh, Eden, Asshur, and Chilmad—also traded with her.

f.g: The city where Abraham once lived.

chapters.n: They supplied fine garments, blue and embroidered cloth, and colorful carpets tied with cords.

f.g: Multicolored carpets or trunks of fine clothing.

chapters.n: Ships of Tarshish carried her goods; she was loaded with cargo and glorious in the heart of the seas.

f.g: Large ocean-going merchant ships.

chapters.n: But her rowers took her into deep water, and the east wind wrecked her. Babylon, from the east, is the storm.

f.w: the east wind hath broken thee

chapters.n: Everything—cargo, crew, captains, carpenters, traders, and soldiers—sinks with her on the day of her ruin.

f.w: shall fall into the midst of the seas

chapters.n: The shorelands shake at the cries of her sailors.

f.g: Pasturelands or coastlands.

chapters.n: Sailors and captains from every ship abandon their vessels and stand on shore.
They cry bitterly, throw dust on their heads, and roll in ashes.

f.w: cast up dust upon their heads

chapters.n: They shave their heads, wear sackcloth, and weep with anguish.

f.g: Shaving the head was a mourning custom.

chapters.n: They lament: “Who was ever like Tyre, now silent in the sea?”
Her trade satisfied many peoples and enriched kings throughout the world.

f.w: thou didst enrich the kings of the earth

chapters.n: Now she lies wrecked in the deep with all her goods and crew.

f.g: Shipwrecked.

chapters.n: Coastland peoples are horrified, and their kings shudder in fear.

f.g: Appalled.

chapters.n: Merchants hiss in shock. Tyre has come to a horrible end and will be no more—showing how quickly worldly wealth and pride can collapse.

f.g: A sound of astonishment or scorn.

chapters.n: Another message, now aimed at Tyre’s ruler.

f.w: The word of the LORD came again unto me
f.g: Chapter 28 targets Tyre’s king, then Sidon.

chapters.n: The prince of Tyre’s pride has swollen until he says, “I am a god, sitting on a divine throne in the heart of the seas.” But he is only a man, however godlike he imagines himself.

f.w: yet thou art a man, and not God

chapters.n: With irony God says: you think you’re wiser than Daniel, that no secret is hidden from you.

f.g: Daniel was known for God-given wisdom in Babylon; some think an ancient sage named Danel is meant.

chapters.n: His business skill brought him gold and silver.
His trading made him rich, and riches made him proud—a pattern the Book of Mormon calls the “pride cycle.”

f.w: thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches

chapters.n: Because he thinks of himself as divine…

f.w: set thine heart as the heart of God
f.g: Considered himself equal to God.

chapters.n: …God will bring the most ruthless of nations against him to pierce his wisdom and defile his splendor.

f.g: The Babylonians.

chapters.n: He will be thrown down to the pit and die a violent death at sea.
Will he still claim to be a god in front of his killer? In that moment he will be shown to be merely mortal.
He will die the shameful death of the uncircumcised—an Israelite way of saying a dishonorable, outcast death—at the hands of foreigners.

f.g: An idiom for dying in disgrace (Phoenicians themselves practiced circumcision).

chapters.n: A new message: a lament for Tyre’s king.

f.w: Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: Verses 11–19 move into language that seems larger than any human king.

chapters.n: The king was the very model of perfection—full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. Many readers, Christian and Latter-day Saint alike, see in this lament a picture of the fall of Lucifer, who also began in glory.

f.g: You were the seal of perfection—the finished model.

f.w: take up a lamentation upon the king of Tyrus

chapters.n: He was in Eden, God’s garden, adorned with precious stones—several of which match the stones on the high priest’s breastplate. Music was part of his creation.

f.w: every precious stone was thy covering

f.g: Tambourines or settings for jewels; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: He was an anointed guardian cherub on God’s holy mountain, walking among fiery stones—imagery of the heavenly court.

f.g: A guardian cherub, like those that covered the ark.

chapters.n: He was blameless from the day of his creation until wickedness was found in him. Evil is not part of God’s creation; it enters by choice.

f.w: till iniquity was found in thee

chapters.n: His vast trade filled him with violence, so God cast him out from the mountain of God as unholy.

f.w: I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain of God

chapters.n: Pride in his beauty corrupted his wisdom. He will be thrown to the earth as a spectacle before kings.

f.w: Thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty
I will cast thee to the ground

chapters.n: Dishonest trade profaned his sanctuaries, so a fire from within him will consume him to ashes before all. Sin carries the seeds of its own destruction.

f.w: I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee
f.g: Destruction from within.

chapters.n: All who knew him will be appalled; he will come to a dreadful end and be no more.

f.w: never shalt thou be any more

chapters.n: A new message about Sidon, Tyre’s older sister city.

f.w: Again the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: A short oracle against Sidon follows.

chapters.n: Ezekiel turns his face against Sidon, about 25 miles north of Tyre.

f.g: Sidon, a Phoenician city that gave its name to Phoenicians generally; home of Jezebel.

chapters.n: God will show his glory and holiness through judgment on Sidon.

f.w: I will be glorified in the midst of thee

chapters.n: Plague and the sword will fill her streets.

f.g: Plague.

chapters.n: Israel will no longer be pricked by hostile neighbors like briers and thorns.
Looking forward: when God gathers Israel from the nations, he will show his holiness through them, and they will live in the land promised to Jacob.

f.w: When I shall have gathered the house of Israel

chapters.n: They will live securely, build houses, and plant vineyards—pictures of peace and permanence—after God judges their hostile neighbors.
Chapters 29–32 contain seven oracles against Egypt. This first is dated January 587 BC, during Jerusalem’s siege, when Judah hoped Egypt would rescue it.

f.w: In the tenth year, in the tenth month, in the twelfth day
f.g: About January 587 BC.

chapters.n: Ezekiel turns against Pharaoh (Hophra) and all Egypt.

f.g: Pharaoh Hophra (Apries), who briefly marched to help Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Pharaoh is pictured as a great crocodile (“dragon”) lying in the Nile channels, boasting, “The Nile is mine; I made it for myself.” He claims credit that belongs to God.

f.g: Hebrew tannin—a sea monster or crocodile.
The Nile, Egypt’s lifeline.

chapters.n: God will hook him by the jaws like a captured crocodile and drag him out, with the fish of the Nile (Egypt’s people) clinging to his scales.

f.w: I will put hooks in thy jaws

chapters.n: He will be tossed into the desert to rot, unburied, food for animals and birds—a shameful end in a culture that prized burial.

f.w: thou shalt not be brought together, nor gathered
f.g: Not gathered for burial.

chapters.n: Egypt has been a “staff of reed” for Israel—something that looks supportive but snaps when leaned on.
When Israel grabbed hold of Egypt, it splintered, tearing their shoulders and making their backs give way. Trusting in the world instead of God leaves us wounded.

f.w: when they leaned upon thee, thou brakest

chapters.n: God will bring a sword against Egypt and cut off people and animals.

f.w: I will bring a sword upon thee

chapters.n: Egypt will be ruined because of Pharaoh’s boast that he made the Nile.

f.w: The river is mine, and I have made it

chapters.n: God will lay Egypt waste from Migdol to Syene (Aswan) and to the border of Cush—its full length, north to south.

f.g: Better “from Migdol to Syene”—from Egypt’s northern frontier to Aswan in the south.
Hebrew Cush—the region of Nubia (modern Sudan).

chapters.n: Neither people nor animals will pass through for forty years—a symbolic generation of judgment, like Israel’s wilderness years.
Egypt will be desolate among desolate lands, and her people scattered among the nations.

f.w: I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations

chapters.n: Yet God will regather Egypt after forty years. Even toward foreign nations, his judgments include mercy.
He will bring them back to Pathros, their ancestral homeland, but as a humble kingdom.

f.g: Upper (southern) Egypt.

chapters.n: Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms, never again ruling over other nations. Historically, after the Persian conquest, Egypt was mostly ruled by foreign powers for centuries.

f.g: The lowliest, least powerful.

chapters.n: Israel will no longer rely on Egypt—a reliance that only reminded God of their lack of faith.

f.w: which bringeth their iniquity to remembrance
f.g: Their trust in Egypt was itself a sin.

chapters.n: This is the latest dated prophecy in Ezekiel: the 27th year, about April 571 BC—sixteen years after the previous verse.

f.g: About 571 BC, the latest date in the book.

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for about 13 years until his soldiers’ heads were rubbed bald and shoulders raw from carrying loads—yet he gained little plunder. Ezekiel honestly records that the outcome at Tyre differed from what one might expect.

f.w: every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled
f.g: From carrying baskets of earth for siege works.
Tyre apparently surrendered on terms after a long siege, leaving little to loot.

chapters.n: So God will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment for his army. Babylon did invade Egypt around 568 BC.

f.w: it shall be the wages for his army

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar unknowingly worked for God, so God pays him with Egypt. God directs even pagan empires.
On that day God will make a “horn” sprout for Israel—new strength, often understood as pointing toward a coming deliverer—and Ezekiel will speak freely among them.

f.w: cause the horn of the house of Israel to bud forth

chapters.n: A second, undated oracle against Egypt.

f.w: The word of the LORD came again unto me
f.g: Verses 1–19 are the only undated oracle against Egypt.

chapters.n: “Wail! Alas for the day!”

f.g: “Alas for the day!”—“worth” is old English for “be.”

chapters.n: The day of the Lord is near—a day of clouds and doom for the nations. The phrase, often used against Israel, now applies to Egypt.

f.w: the day of the LORD is near

chapters.n: A sword will strike Egypt, and Cush (Nubia) will writhe in anguish as Egypt’s people are carried off and its foundations torn down.

f.g: Cush, south of Egypt.

chapters.n: Egypt’s allies—Cush, Put, Lud, Arabia, Libya, and others in league—will fall with her.

f.g: Unknown; perhaps Libya (Lub).

f.w: the men of the land that is in league
f.g: Possibly “the people of the covenant land”—even Jews living in Egypt.

chapters.n: Those who support Egypt will fall; her proud power will collapse from Migdol to Syene.
Egypt will lie desolate among other ruined lands.

f.w: desolate in the midst of the countries that are desolate

chapters.n: When God sets Egypt on fire and her helpers are crushed, they will know he is the Lord.

f.w: I have set a fire in Egypt

chapters.n: Messengers will go out by ship (up the Nile) to terrify complacent Cush.

f.w: messengers go forth from me in ships

f.g: Complacent, feeling secure.

chapters.n: God will end Egypt’s hordes through Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon.
He and his ruthless army will come to destroy the land and fill it with the slain.
God will dry up the Nile’s channels and sell the land to evil men. Without the Nile, Egypt cannot live.

f.w: I will make the rivers dry

chapters.n: Idols will be destroyed in Memphis, and there will be no more native prince over Egypt. Indeed, after the Persian conquest, foreign rulers governed Egypt for most of its history for many centuries.

f.g: Memphis, ancient capital of Egypt near modern Cairo.

f.w: there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt
f.g: No more native Egyptian ruler.

chapters.n: Judgment will fall city by city: Pathros (Upper Egypt), Zoan (Tanis), and No (Thebes).

f.g: Tanis, in the Nile Delta.
Thebes (modern Luxor), Upper Egypt’s great capital.

chapters.n: God’s fury will fall on Sin (Pelusium), Egypt’s border fortress, and on the crowds of Thebes.

f.g: Pelusium, a fortress guarding Egypt’s northeast frontier.

chapters.n: Fire in Egypt: Pelusium will writhe, Thebes will be breached, and Memphis will face constant distress.

f.g: Broken open.

chapters.n: The young men of On (Heliopolis) and Pi-beseth (Bubastis) will die, and the cities’ people go captive.

f.g: On or Heliopolis, center of sun worship; “Aven” means “wickedness,” a pun.
Bubastis, a Delta city devoted to a cat goddess.

chapters.n: At Tahpanhes, where Jewish refugees (including Jeremiah) had fled, the day will turn dark when Egypt’s power is broken.

f.g: Tahpanhes, a frontier city in the eastern Delta.

chapters.n: Thus God will judge Egypt, and they will know he is the Lord.
A new dated oracle: April 587 BC, about three months after 29:1, shortly after Babylon drove back Pharaoh’s relief army.

f.w: in the eleventh year, in the first month, in the seventh day
f.g: About April 587 BC.

chapters.n: God has broken Pharaoh’s arm, and it won’t be bandaged or splinted to hold a sword again. Pharaoh Hophra’s attempt to relieve Jerusalem had failed.

f.w: I have broken the arm of Pharaoh

f.g: A bandage.

chapters.n: God will break both his arms—the strong one and the injured one—so the sword falls from his hand.

f.w: the strong, and that which was broken
f.g: Total loss of military power.

chapters.n: The Egyptians will be scattered among the nations.
God will strengthen Babylon’s arms and put his own sword in its hand, while Pharaoh groans like a mortally wounded man.

f.w: put my sword in his hand

chapters.n: Babylon’s arms will be strong and Pharaoh’s will drop. Then all will know that the Lord, not Babylon’s gods, directed history.

f.w: he shall stretch it out upon the land of Egypt

chapters.n: The oracle closes as it began, with scattering and the recognition of the Lord.

f.w: they shall know that I am the LORD

chapters.n: Dated June 587 BC, this oracle uses an allegory of a great tree to warn Pharaoh.

f.w: in the eleventh year, in the third month, in the first day
f.g: About June 587 BC.

chapters.n: God asks Pharaoh: Who are you like in your greatness? Consider a lesson from history.

f.w: Whom art thou like in thy greatness?
f.g: A rhetorical question setting up the comparison.

chapters.n: Assyria was once like a towering cedar of Lebanon with beautiful branches and shade, its top among the clouds. Yet Assyria had fallen in 612–609 BC.

f.w: the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon
f.g: Some scholars read “cypress” instead of “Assyria,” making the tree itself Egypt; either way, the fall of a great empire is the lesson.
Thick, shady foliage.

chapters.n: Deep waters nourished it, and streams flowed around it to all the trees of the field—the empire’s wealth and power.

f.w: the deep set him up on high
f.g: Underground waters made it grow tall.

chapters.n: So it grew taller than every other tree, with spreading branches.

f.w: his height was exalted above all the trees

chapters.n: Birds nested in its boughs, animals bore young beneath it, and great nations lived in its shade—the empire sheltered many peoples.

f.w: All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs

chapters.n: It was magnificent because its roots reached abundant water.

f.w: his root was by great waters

chapters.n: Even the trees in Eden, God’s garden, could not rival it.

f.g: Probably plane trees.

chapters.n: God made it beautiful—its glory was a gift—and all Eden’s trees envied it.

f.g: Its greatness came from God.

chapters.n: But because it grew proud of its height, its heart was lifted up.

f.w: his heart is lifted up in his height

chapters.n: So God handed it to a mighty ruler of the nations—Babylon—who dealt with it as its wickedness deserved.

f.w: the mighty one of the heathen
f.g: Nebuchadnezzar or the Babylonian-Median alliance that defeated Assyria.

chapters.n: Ruthless foreigners cut it down. Its branches lie across mountains and valleys, and the nations abandon its shade.
Birds and beasts now sit on its fallen trunk and branches—where they once found shelter, now they find a carcass.
The lesson: no tree, however well-watered, should exalt itself. All are destined for death, going down to the pit like ordinary mortals.

f.w: the nether parts of the earth
f.g: The underworld, the realm of the dead.

f.w: they are all delivered unto death

chapters.n: When it fell, God made the deep mourn and the waters stop; Lebanon and all trees grieved. Its fall affected the whole world.

f.g: Creation itself mourns the fall.

chapters.n: The nations shook at its fall as God cast it down to Sheol. The other fallen trees of Eden were comforted to see the mighty one join them.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the grave, the realm of the dead, not necessarily a place of punishment.

chapters.n: Its allies who lived in its shade went down to Sheol with it.

f.g: Its allies and supporters.

chapters.n: Now God applies the lesson: Pharaoh, which tree in Eden are you like? You too will be brought down to lie among the uncircumcised and the slain. “This is Pharaoh.”

f.w: This is Pharaoh and all his multitude
f.g: The allegory is applied directly to Egypt.

f.w: in the midst of the uncircumcised

chapters.n: Dated March 585 BC—after Jerusalem had fallen—this is a funeral lament for Pharaoh.

f.w: in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day
f.g: About March 585 BC.

chapters.n: Pharaoh saw himself as a young lion among nations, but he is really a sea monster thrashing in the Nile, churning and muddying the waters—causing chaos rather than order.

f.w: a young lion of the nations

f.g: Hebrew tannin—a sea monster or crocodile, as in 29:3.

chapters.n: God will throw his net over Pharaoh using many peoples and haul him out.

f.w: I will therefore spread out my net over thee

chapters.n: He will be flung onto dry land as food for birds and beasts.

f.w: I will cast thee forth upon the open field

chapters.n: His enormous carcass will cover mountains and fill valleys—exaggerated imagery of total defeat.

f.g: Possibly “your rotting remains”—the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: His blood will soak the land up to the mountains and fill the streams.

f.w: the rivers shall be full of thee
f.g: Recalls the Nile turned to blood in Moses’ day.

chapters.n: When his light is snuffed out, God will darken the sky—sun, moon, and stars. Cosmic darkness is a recurring image for the day of the Lord.

f.w: I will cover the sun with a cloud

chapters.n: All the bright lights of heaven will go dark over Egypt—fitting for a land that worshipped the sun god Ra.
Many peoples will be troubled when news of Egypt’s fall spreads to distant lands.

f.g: Trouble, disturb.

chapters.n: Kings will shudder and tremble for their own lives when God brandishes his sword.

f.w: they shall tremble at every moment

chapters.n: Plainly stated: Babylon’s sword is coming against Egypt.

f.w: The sword of the king of Babylon

chapters.n: Egypt’s pride and its crowds will be crushed by the most ruthless of nations.

f.g: Egypt’s pride and splendor.

chapters.n: Even its cattle will be gone, so no foot or hoof will muddy the waters anymore.

f.w: neither shall the foot of man trouble them

chapters.n: With nothing stirring them, the waters will settle and flow smoothly like oil—an eerie calm over an empty land.

f.w: cause their rivers to run like oil
f.g: Still, clear, and slow-moving.

chapters.n: When Egypt is emptied and struck, they will know the Lord.

f.w: destitute of that whereof it was full
f.g: Stripped of its abundance.

chapters.n: This lament will be chanted by the women of the nations, as professional mourners did at funerals.

f.w: the daughters of the nations shall lament her

chapters.n: Two weeks later (in the same year) comes a final oracle: a vision of Egypt descending to the realm of the dead.

f.w: in the fifteenth day of the month
f.g: Probably of the twelfth month, two weeks after v. 1.

chapters.n: Ezekiel is to wail for Egypt and, by his prophetic word, send her down to the underworld with other great nations.

f.g: The prophet’s word accomplishes what it announces.

chapters.n: “Are you more beautiful than anyone? Go down and lie with the uncircumcised!” Egypt’s pride counts for nothing in death.

f.w: Whom dost thou pass in beauty?

chapters.n: Egypt will fall among those killed by the sword and be dragged away with her multitudes.

f.g: Drag her off.

chapters.n: The mighty dead in Sheol will greet Pharaoh and his allies: “They have come down; they lie with the uncircumcised.”

f.w: out of the midst of hell
f.g: From Sheol, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: Assyria is there, surrounded by the graves of her soldiers, all killed by the sword.

f.g: Assyria, the empire that fell in 612–609 BC.

chapters.n: Her graves lie in the deepest part of the pit. She once spread terror among the living; now she lies with the slain.

f.g: The farthest depths of the underworld.

chapters.n: Elam (in western Iran) is there too, once terrifying, now bearing shame with the dead.

f.g: An ancient kingdom east of Babylon, conquered by Assyria.

chapters.n: Elam lies on a bed among the slain, her shame now complete.

f.w: They have set her a bed
f.g: Her place in the grave.

chapters.n: Meshech and Tubal, warlike peoples of Asia Minor, are there as well.

f.g: Peoples of Anatolia; they reappear in chapters 38–39 with Gog.

chapters.n: They do not receive the honorable burial of ancient heroes, who were buried with weapons under their heads. Their sins rest on their bones.

f.w: they have laid their swords under their heads
f.g: Honored warriors were buried with their weapons.

chapters.n: Pharaoh, you too will be broken and lie among the uncircumcised and the slain.
Edom, its kings, and princes lie there, despite all their might.
So do the princes of the north and the Sidonians—ashamed of the power that once caused terror.

f.g: Probably Phoenician and Syrian rulers.

chapters.n: Pharaoh will see them and find grim “comfort” that he is not alone in his fall.

f.g: Consoled in a bitter sense—misery has company.

chapters.n: God allowed Pharaoh to spread terror in the land of the living, but in the end he will lie among the slain. Earthly power always ends, but God’s purposes do not. The oracles against the nations end here.

f.w: I have caused my terror in the land of the living
f.g: Some manuscripts read “his terror.”

chapters.n: Chapter 33 is a turning point. Before news of Jerusalem’s fall arrives, God renews Ezekiel’s call as a watchman (compare 3:16–21). From here the book shifts toward hope and restoration.

f.w: Again the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: When war threatens, a city chooses one of its own as a watchman to stand on the wall and look for danger.
If he sees an army coming, he blows the trumpet to warn everyone.

f.g: The shofar, a ram’s-horn trumpet used to sound alarms.

chapters.n: Anyone who hears the alarm but ignores it is responsible for his own death.

f.w: his blood shall be upon his own head

chapters.n: He heard and did nothing, so his blood is on him. But anyone who listens saves his life.

f.w: he that taketh warning shall deliver his soul

chapters.n: But if the watchman sees danger and stays silent, people still die in their sins—yet God holds the watchman responsible.

f.w: his blood will I require at the watchman's hand

chapters.n: God has made Ezekiel that watchman for Israel. He must listen to God and pass the warning on. Latter-day Saint leaders and members are likewise taught to warn their neighbors with love.

f.w: I have set thee a watchman

chapters.n: If God declares a wicked person will die and Ezekiel doesn’t warn him, Ezekiel shares the guilt.

f.w: O wicked man, thou shalt surely die

chapters.n: If he warns and they don’t turn, Ezekiel has saved himself.
The exiles are now crushed by guilt: “Our sins weigh on us and we are wasting away—how can we live?” For the first time they admit their sin—and despair.
God answers despair with hope: he swears he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but wants them to turn and live. “Turn, turn—why will you die?”

f.w: I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked
turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways

chapters.n: Past righteousness won’t save someone who turns to sin, and past wickedness won’t condemn someone who turns from it. What matters is the direction you are now facing.

f.w: he shall not fall thereby in the day that he turneth from his wickedness

chapters.n: If a righteous person trusts in his own goodness as a license to sin, his past good deeds won’t be remembered.

f.w: if he trust to his own righteousness

chapters.n: But if a wicked person turns from sin and does what is right…

f.w: if he turn from his sin

chapters.n: …returning collateral, repaying what he stole, and walking in the laws that give life, he will surely live. Real repentance includes restitution where possible.

f.w: give again that he had robbed
f.g: Restitution—returning what was taken.

chapters.n: None of his past sins will be held against him. He will live.

f.w: None of his sins that he hath committed shall be mentioned unto him

chapters.n: Some still say God isn’t fair—but it is their ways that are unfair.

f.w: The way of the Lord is not equal

chapters.n: A righteous person who turns to evil will die for it.
A wicked person who turns to righteousness will live because of it.
God will judge each person by his own ways.

f.w: I will judge you every one after his ways

chapters.n: The long-awaited moment: in the twelfth year, a refugee from Jerusalem arrives and reports, “The city has fallen!” The journey from Jerusalem to Babylon took several months.

f.w: in the twelfth year of our captivity, in the tenth month
f.g: About January 585 BC, roughly five months after the city fell (some manuscripts read the eleventh year).

chapters.n: The evening before the messenger arrived, God’s hand came on Ezekiel and opened his mouth. His years of restricted speech ended, just as God had promised.
God speaks to Ezekiel again.

f.w: Then the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: His first message after the news of the fall.

chapters.n: Survivors living among the ruins in Judah boasted: “Abraham was just one man and he got the land; we are many, so surely it’s ours.” They claimed Abraham’s promise without Abraham’s faith.

f.w: Abraham was one, and he inherited the land

chapters.n: God replies: you eat meat with the blood in it, worship idols, and murder—and you expect to own the land?
You rely on your swords, do detestable things, and commit adultery—should you own the land? Covenant blessings require covenant faithfulness.

f.g: You rely on violence.

chapters.n: Those in the ruins will die by sword, wild beasts, and disease—even in fortresses and caves.

f.w: the forts and in the caves
f.g: Places where survivors hid.

chapters.n: The land will be utterly desolate, its proud strength ended, its mountains empty of travelers.
Then they will know the Lord, when the land lies waste because of their abominations.
Ezekiel has become popular. People chat about him by the walls and in doorways: “Let’s go hear what the Lord says today!”

f.g: Or “talking about you.”

chapters.n: They come and sit before him like devoted followers and listen—but they don’t do what he says. Their words are full of affection, but their hearts are set on gain.

f.w: they hear thy words, but they will not do them
with their mouth they shew much love

chapters.n: To them Ezekiel is like a singer with a beautiful voice performing love songs—enjoyable entertainment, but not something to act on.

f.w: a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice
f.g: Probably “a love song.”

chapters.n: But when what he says comes to pass—and it will—they will know a prophet has been among them.

f.w: shall they know that a prophet hath been among them

chapters.n: Chapter 34 contrasts Israel’s selfish leaders with the Lord, the true Shepherd. Jesus drew on this chapter when he called himself the Good Shepherd.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: “Shepherds” in the ancient Near East meant kings and leaders. Woe to Israel’s shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock!

f.g: Kings, officials, and other leaders.

f.w: should not the shepherds feed the flocks?

chapters.n: They eat the best, wear the wool, and slaughter the fattest sheep, but never care for the flock. Leadership became a way to profit.

They haven’t strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bandaged the injured, brought back strays, or searched for the lost. Instead they ruled harshly. This is a clear description of what true ministering looks like.

f.w: neither have ye sought that which was lost
with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them

chapters.n: Without a real shepherd, the sheep scattered and became prey to wild animals—the nations.

f.w: scattered, because there is no shepherd

chapters.n: God’s sheep wandered over every mountain and were scattered across the earth, and no one searched for them.

f.w: none did search or seek after them

chapters.n: So, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord.

f.g: The indictment turns to sentence.

chapters.n: God swears: because his flock became prey while the shepherds fed only themselves…

f.g: God repeatedly calls Israel his own flock.

chapters.n: …shepherds, listen!

f.w: hear the word of the LORD
f.g: The repetition adds emphasis.

chapters.n: God is against these shepherds. He will hold them accountable for his sheep and remove them from leadership, rescuing his flock from their mouths.

f.w: I will require my flock at their hand

chapters.n: Then the great promise: “I, even I, will search for my sheep and seek them out.” The Lord himself will come as Shepherd. Latter-day Saints recognize this Shepherd as Jehovah, Jesus Christ.

f.w: I, even I, will both search my sheep

chapters.n: As a shepherd gathers his scattered flock, God will rescue them from every place they were scattered on that dark, cloudy day—the day of Jerusalem’s fall.
He will bring them out of the nations, gather them, and pasture them on Israel’s mountains by its streams—the promise of gathering.
Good grazing land and secure folds on Israel’s high mountains—the picture recalls Psalm 23.

f.w: I will feed them in a good pasture

chapters.n: “I myself will feed my flock and give them rest.”

f.w: I will cause them to lie down

chapters.n: God will do everything the bad shepherds failed to do: seek the lost, bring back the strays, bandage the hurt, strengthen the weak. But the fat and strong who exploit others he will judge.

f.w: I will seek that which was lost
I will feed them with judgment
f.g: Or “I will shepherd them with justice.”

chapters.n: Now God speaks to the flock itself: he will judge between sheep and sheep, rams and goats. Jesus later used this image of separating sheep and goats.

f.w: between the rams and the he goats

chapters.n: Some sheep not only eat the best grass but trample the rest; they drink clear water and muddy what’s left. Selfishness isn’t limited to leaders.

f.w: tread down with your feet the residue of your pastures

chapters.n: The weaker sheep must eat what was trampled and drink what was muddied.

f.w: they eat that which ye have trodden
f.g: The poor live with the leftovers of the powerful.

chapters.n: God himself will judge between the fat and the lean.

f.w: the fat cattle and between the lean cattle

chapters.n: The strong pushed the weak aside with shoulder and horn until they were scattered.

f.w: pushed all the diseased with your horns

chapters.n: God will save his flock so they are no longer prey, and he will judge between sheep.

God will set one shepherd over them—“my servant David.” David had died centuries earlier, so this points to a future king from David’s line: the Messiah. Christians see its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.
The Lord will be their God, and David his prince among them. God and his anointed rule together.
He will make a “covenant of peace” and rid the land of dangerous animals, so his sheep can sleep safely even in wilderness and forest.

f.w: cause the evil beasts to cease

chapters.n: His people and the area around his holy hill will be a blessing; rain will come in its season—“showers of blessing.”

f.w: there shall be showers of blessing

f.g: Mount Zion, God’s holy hill.

chapters.n: Trees and fields will be fruitful, and they will be safe. They’ll know God when he breaks their yoke and frees them from those who enslaved them.

f.w: broken the bands of their yoke

chapters.n: No longer prey to nations or beasts, they will live in safety with no one to make them afraid.
God will give them a land renowned for its crops—or, as some read it, a “plant of renown” pointing to the Messiah, the righteous Branch. Hunger and shame will end.

f.g: Possibly a famous planting or harvest; many see a messianic hint.

chapters.n: They will know that the Lord their God is with them and that Israel is his people.

f.w: I the LORD their God am with them

chapters.n: “You are my flock, the sheep of my pasture; you are people, and I am your God.” A tender close: God’s care for his people is personal.
Before promising restoration to Israel’s mountains (ch. 36), God pronounces judgment on Mount Seir—Edom—which hoped to seize Israel’s land.

f.w: Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Ezekiel turns his face against Mount Seir, the mountainous homeland of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

f.g: The highlands of Edom, home of Esau’s descendants.

chapters.n: God is against Seir and will stretch out his hand to make it utterly desolate.

f.w: I will stretch out mine hand against thee

chapters.n: Edom’s towns will be ruined, and it will know the Lord.

f.w: I will lay thy cities waste

chapters.n: Edom nursed an ancient, endless hatred—going back to Jacob and Esau—and attacked Israel at its lowest moment, when Jerusalem fell.

f.w: in the time of their calamity

chapters.n: Since Edom did not hate bloodshed, bloodshed will pursue it. A play on words: Edom (’edom) and blood (dam) sound alike in Hebrew.

f.g: Since.
A pun on Edom’s name and the Hebrew for blood.

chapters.n: Seir will become so desolate that no one comes or goes.

f.w: him that passeth out and him that returneth
f.g: Travelers in either direction.

chapters.n: Its hills, valleys, and ravines will be filled with the slain.

f.w: I will fill his mountains with his slain men

chapters.n: Edom will be a permanent ruin. Historically, the Edomites were pushed out of their homeland by Arab tribes (the Nabateans) and later absorbed into Judea; Edom as a nation disappeared.

f.w: I will make thee perpetual desolations

chapters.n: Edom boasted that both nations—Israel and Judah—would become its property. But it forgot that the Lord was there. The land belongs to God.

f.w: These two nations and these two countries shall be mine
f.g: The former northern and southern kingdoms.

chapters.n: God will repay Edom according to its own anger and envy, and make himself known through that judgment.
God heard every insult Edom spoke about Israel’s mountains: “They are desolate—ours to devour!”

f.w: I have heard all thy blasphemies

chapters.n: In boasting against Israel, Edom was really boasting against God, and he heard it all.

f.w: with your mouth ye have boasted against me

chapters.n: While the whole earth rejoices, Edom will be desolate.

f.g: Possibly “as the whole earth rejoiced (at your fall).”

chapters.n: As Edom rejoiced over Israel’s ruin, so it will be ruined—a principle of measure-for-measure justice. Then Ezekiel turns, in chapter 36, to the restoration of Israel’s mountains.

f.g: The Greek name for Edom.

chapters.n: Chapter 35 condemned Edom’s mountains; now Ezekiel speaks a message of hope to the mountains of Israel themselves. The land is addressed like a person who has suffered and will be comforted.

f.g: The Lord’s usual title for Ezekiel—a reminder that he is a mortal sent with God’s word.

chapters.n: Israel’s enemies gloated after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, crowing that even Israel’s ancient hills now belonged to them. The Lord takes their taunt personally.
