f.g: A cry of gloating at someone else’s misfortune.
Hilltops; here simply the high ground of the land, claimed as plunder.

chapters.n: The neighbors had stripped the land bare and turned Israel into a joke and a byword. To be “taken up in the lips of talkers” means to become the subject of gossip and mockery.

f.g: The remaining nations nearby—Edom, Ammon, Moab, Philistia.
Disgrace, bad reputation.

chapters.n: The Lord addresses every part of the land—hills, streams, valleys, ruined towns—as if calling each one by name. None of the devastated places is forgotten.

f.g: Scorn, ridicule.

chapters.n: God’s “jealousy” here is His protective zeal for His people and land. Edom (Idumea) especially rejoiced to seize Judah’s territory after the Babylonian conquest.

f.g: The Greek form of Edom, the nation descended from Esau.
Hebrew qinʾah—intense, protective zeal, not petty envy.

chapters.n: Israel has endured the shame heaped on it by the nations. The Lord now declares that He has heard and will act.

f.w: borne the shame of the heathen

chapters.n: Lifting the hand was a gesture of solemn oath. The Lord swears that the mockers will themselves experience the shame they poured on Israel.

f.w: I have lifted up mine hand
f.g: An oath gesture, like raising the hand to swear.

chapters.n: A turning point: the barren mountains will sprout and bear fruit again, because God’s people are about to come home. The land itself prepares for the return.

f.w: they are at hand to come
f.g: The return is near—fulfilled in part after Cyrus’s decree (538 BC) and, Latter-day Saints believe, more fully in the latter-day gathering.

chapters.n: “I am for you”—after years of judgment, God declares Himself on the land’s side. Fields that lay wild will be plowed and planted again.

f.g: The reverse of “I am against thee” spoken to Edom and others.

chapters.n: The whole house of Israel—not only Judah but all the tribes—will fill the land again, and ruined towns will be rebuilt.

f.w: all the house of Israel, even all of it

chapters.n: God promises not merely restoration but something better than Israel’s beginnings. The repeated refrain “ye shall know that I am the LORD” shows the goal: that people will come to know Him.

f.w: will do better unto you than at your beginnings
ye shall know that I am the LORD
f.g: Ezekiel’s signature phrase, used more than 60 times.

chapters.n: The land that once seemed to swallow its inhabitants through war and famine will become a safe inheritance where Israel’s children are no longer lost.

f.g: Leave them childless; take away their people.

chapters.n: Outsiders had said the land was cursed—a land that “eats” its people. The spies in Moses’ day had used almost the same words.
The Lord reverses that reputation. The land will no longer be known for death and loss.
Israel will no longer hear the taunts of the nations or stumble into the sins that brought its downfall.

f.g: Insult, disgrace.

chapters.n: A new message begins. Having promised to restore the land, the Lord now explains why Israel lost it and what He will do to change Israel’s heart.
Israel’s own behavior made the land ritually unclean. The comparison uses the Law of Moses’ language of ritual impurity to show how serious their sins had become.

f.g: A woman set apart during menstruation, considered ritually unclean under the Law of Moses.

chapters.n: Violence and idolatry were the two great sins that brought the exile. Innocent blood and false worship polluted the land God had given them.

f.w: the blood that they had shed

chapters.n: Scattering among the nations was the consequence Moses had warned of. God’s judgment matched their conduct.

f.w: I scattered them among the heathen

chapters.n: Even in exile, Israel dishonored God. The nations sneered, “These are supposed to be the Lord’s people, yet they were thrown out of His land”—making God look weak or unfaithful.

f.g: Brought disrespect on God’s reputation.

chapters.n: The Lord’s concern is for His “name”—His character and reputation among all peoples. His mercy flows from who He is.
Israel’s restoration will not be a reward for their goodness; it flows from God’s own faithfulness and holiness. This is grace: undeserved help given for His name’s sake.
When God restores and transforms His people, the nations will see His holiness displayed in them. A changed people becomes the evidence of a living God.

f.w: I shall be sanctified in you
f.g: God’s holiness will be shown openly through what He does in Israel.

chapters.n: The gathering: God will bring Israel out of every land back to its own. Latter-day Saints see both the ancient return and the modern gathering of Israel in this promise.

f.w: gather you out of all countries
f.r: Ezekiel 37:21; Isaiah 11:11-12; 3 Nephi 20:29; Articles of Faith 1:10

chapters.n: Sprinkled water was used in the Law of Moses for purification. Here it pictures God Himself washing away sin and idolatry; many Christians see an image of baptism and spiritual cleansing.

One of the great promises of the Old Testament: God will replace a hard, unresponsive “heart of stone” with a living, feeling “heart of flesh.” True change comes from the inside, and God is the one who brings it about.

f.w: A new heart also will I give you

f.g: A heart that is hard, cold, and unable to respond to God.

chapters.n: God’s own Spirit will dwell in them and empower them to obey. Obedience becomes the fruit of a changed heart, not a burden imposed from outside.

f.w: I will put my spirit within you

chapters.n: The covenant formula—“ye shall be my people, and I will be your God”—sums up the relationship God has always wanted with Israel.

f.w: ye shall be my people, and I will be your God

chapters.n: The Lord promises both spiritual and physical blessings: cleansing from sin and abundant grain with no famine. “Corn” in the KJV means grain in general, not maize.

f.g: Grain such as wheat or barley.

chapters.n: Fruitful trees and fields will end the shame of famine that made Israel a laughingstock. God’s blessing on the land will be visible to everyone.
Grace leads to genuine repentance. When Israel sees how good God has been, they will look back on their sins with honest sorrow and disgust.

f.g: Loathe—feel deep shame and revulsion at your own past behavior.

chapters.n: The Lord repeats that He acts for His name’s sake, not because Israel earned it. Humility is the right response to unearned mercy.

f.g: Embarrassed, put to shame.

chapters.n: Cleansing comes first, then rebuilding. Spiritual renewal precedes the restoration of cities and homes.
Travelers who once passed a wasteland will see cultivated fields. The change will be obvious to everyone.
People will compare the restored land to the garden of Eden—a picture of paradise regained. The ruined cities will be fortified and full of people again.

f.g: Fortified with walls.

chapters.n: The restoration will prove to the surrounding nations that Israel’s God keeps His word. “I the LORD have spoken it, and I will do it” is a guarantee.

f.w: I the LORD have spoken it, and I will do it

chapters.n: Though God has promised all this, He still invites Israel to ask Him for it. Prayer is part of how His promises are fulfilled.

f.w: I will yet for this be inquired of

chapters.n: At Jerusalem’s great festivals, the city overflowed with flocks of sacrificial animals. In the same way, the empty cities will overflow with people.

f.g: The appointed holy festivals such as Passover and Tabernacles.

chapters.n: Ezekiel is carried in a vision by the Spirit to a valley strewn with bones—perhaps the scene of an ancient battle where the dead were never buried. “The hand of the LORD” signals a powerful revelatory experience.

f.w: The hand of the LORD was upon me
in the spirit of the LORD

chapters.n: God walks Ezekiel all around the valley so he can see how many bones there are and how completely dead they are. Humanly speaking, the situation is hopeless.

f.g: Long dead—no trace of life remains.

chapters.n: “Can these bones live?” Ezekiel’s wise answer neither doubts nor presumes: only God knows what God can do.
The prophet is told to preach to dead bones—an absurd task unless God’s word itself carries life-giving power.

f.w: hear the word of the LORD

chapters.n: The Hebrew word ruach means breath, wind, and spirit, and this chapter plays on all three meanings. God promises to put breath back into the dead.

f.g: Hebrew ruach—breath, wind, or spirit; the same word appears throughout this vision.

chapters.n: The order follows the human body—sinews, flesh, skin, then breath. Like the creation of Adam, the body is formed first and then given life.

f.g: Tendons and ligaments that hold bones together.

chapters.n: As Ezekiel obeys, there is a rattling, and bones snap into place, each to its proper partner. God’s word is already working.

f.g: Or “a rattling”; Hebrew raʿash, also used for an earthquake.

chapters.n: The bodies are complete but still lifeless. The vision shows two stages: physical restoration, then the gift of life.
Ezekiel is told to summon the breath from the four winds—from every direction. God’s Spirit is the true source of life.

f.w: Come from the four winds, O breath

chapters.n: Breath enters, and the dead stand up as a vast army. Latter-day Saints also see in this vision a vivid picture of the literal resurrection, when spirit and body are reunited.

f.w: they lived, and stood up upon their feet

chapters.n: God interprets the vision. The bones are exiled Israel, who feel dead, hopeless, and cut off. Ezekiel’s audience in Babylon was quoting its own despair back to God.

f.g: “We are completely cut off”—a cry of despair.

chapters.n: Their “graves” are the lands of exile. God promises to open them and bring His people home—a national resurrection that also points to the literal resurrection of the dead.
When Israel is raised and returned, they will finally recognize the Lord’s power and love. The tender phrase “O my people” is repeated.
The climax: God will put His own Spirit in them. Physical return is not enough; true life comes when God’s Spirit dwells in His people.

f.w: shall put my spirit in you

f.g: God both promises and carries out what He says.

chapters.n: A second revelation follows, this time an object lesson Ezekiel is to act out.

Ezekiel writes on two sticks (or wooden tablets): one for Judah, one for Joseph through Ephraim. In history, these represent the southern and northern kingdoms. Latter-day Saints also understand them as records—the Bible (record of Judah) and the Book of Mormon (record of Joseph).

f.g: Hebrew ʿets—wood; possibly a wooden writing board, as used in the ancient Near East.

f.w: For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim

chapters.n: Joined end to end in Ezekiel’s hand, the two sticks look like one. Israel, long divided, will be united—and Latter-day Saints see the two records growing together as one witness of Christ.

f.w: they shall become one in thine hand

chapters.n: The exiles will ask what this strange act means. Ezekiel’s symbolic actions were designed to provoke questions.

f.w: Wilt thou not shew us what thou meanest

chapters.n: God Himself will join Joseph’s stick with Judah’s. The unity is His work, not merely a human arrangement.

f.w: they shall be one in mine hand

chapters.n: Ezekiel holds the sticks up before the people—a visible, memorable sign of the promise.
Gathering again: God will bring the scattered children of Israel from every nation back to their land.
Israel had been split into two kingdoms since about 930 BC. God promises that the division will end under one king.

f.w: they shall be no more two nations

chapters.n: Unity will come with purity. A gathered people will also be a cleansed people, free from idols.

f.g: Idols and their associated practices.

chapters.n: “David my servant” cannot be David himself, who had died centuries earlier. It refers to a future king from David’s line—fulfilled supremely in Jesus Christ, the Good Shepherd.

f.w: David my servant shall be king over them

chapters.n: The promised land is a lasting inheritance for generation after generation, under the rule of the Davidic prince forever.

A “covenant of peace” and “everlasting covenant” brings God’s sanctuary—His temple presence—into their midst. Latter-day Saints connect the everlasting covenant with the restored gospel and temple blessings.
God will dwell among His people. John’s Revelation echoes this promise as the ultimate destiny of the faithful.

f.w: My tabernacle also shall be with them

chapters.n: The presence of God’s temple among Israel will show the world that He has made them holy. The chapter ends with the theme that runs through Ezekiel’s final chapters: God’s presence returning to His people.

f.g: Make holy; set apart for God.

chapters.n: A new prophecy opens two chapters about a great final enemy. After promises of gathering and peace (chapters 36–37), the Lord reveals that a last assault will come against His restored people.

Gog is a mysterious leader from the far north; Magog is his land, and Meshech and Tubal were peoples in what is now Turkey. Many readers see Gog as a symbol of all the nations that will oppose God’s people in the last days.

f.g: Some translations read “prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal,” taking Rosh as a place name.

chapters.n: God declares Himself against Gog. However mighty this coalition seems, its true opponent is the Lord.
Hooks in the jaws picture a captured beast led wherever its master chooses. Gog thinks he is acting freely, but God is steering events.

f.g: Small round shields.

chapters.n: Allies come from the edges of the known world: Persia to the east, Ethiopia (Cush) and Libya (Put) to the south. The point is a worldwide alliance against Israel.

f.g: Hebrew Cush—the region south of Egypt.
Hebrew Put—a people of North Africa.

chapters.n: Gomer and Togarmah were northern peoples listed among Japheth’s descendants. North and south, east and west join the attack.
With irony, the Lord tells Gog to get ready and lead his troops well. However prepared they are, they will fail.

f.w: be thou a guard unto them
f.g: Be their commander or protector.

chapters.n: The timing: “in the latter years,” after Israel has been gathered from many nations and lives in safety. Latter-day Saints associate this with the events before the Second Coming.

f.g: Restored after war and exile.

chapters.n: Gog’s armies sweep in like a storm cloud covering the land—an image of overwhelming numbers.
Gog’s plan begins in his own mind: greed and malice lead him to devise an evil scheme.

f.w: thou shalt think an evil thought

chapters.n: Gathered Israel lives peacefully in open villages without defensive walls—trusting in God. Gog sees them as easy targets.

f.g: Heavy beams used to lock city gates.

chapters.n: Gog’s motive is plunder: the gathered people have rebuilt ruined places and prospered, and he wants their wealth.

f.w: in the midst of the land
f.g: Literally “the navel of the earth”—Israel pictured as the world’s center.

chapters.n: Trading nations—Sheba and Dedan in Arabia, Tarshish in the far west—watch with interest, perhaps hoping to profit from the spoils.

f.g: A distant seaport, probably in Spain; a symbol of far-off trade.
Strong men or rulers; possibly the merchants’ bold leaders.

chapters.n: The Lord asks Gog: when My people are living safely, will you not notice and seize the opportunity? He knows Gog’s heart before Gog acts.
Gog comes from the far north with a huge cavalry. In the Bible, “the north” often stands for the direction from which invasion comes.
God brings Gog against His land for a purpose: so that when Gog falls, the nations will recognize God’s holiness and power.

f.w: I shall be sanctified in thee
f.g: God’s holiness will be displayed by His judgment on Gog.

chapters.n: The Lord asks whether Gog is the enemy that earlier prophets had warned would come. The question links Gog to many prophecies of a final attack on God’s people.
When Gog attacks Israel, God’s anger rises in His face—an image of a protector’s fierce reaction to an assault on those He loves.

f.w: my fury shall come up in my face
f.g: Literally “in my nostrils”—a Hebrew image of flaring anger.

chapters.n: A great earthquake will shake the land of Israel. Earthquakes often accompany God’s coming in scripture.
All creation—fish, birds, animals, humans—trembles before God’s presence. Mountains collapse and walls fall.
In panic, Gog’s armies will turn on one another—a pattern seen in Israel’s history when God fought for His people.

f.w: every man's sword shall be against his brother

chapters.n: God fights with the forces of nature: disease, torrential rain, hail, fire, and burning sulfur—like the judgment on Sodom and the plagues of Egypt.

f.g: Enter into judgment against him.

chapters.n: The purpose of it all: the nations will come to know that the Lord is God. Even judgment serves to reveal Him.

f.g: Show My greatness.

chapters.n: The prophecy against Gog continues, repeating the Lord’s declaration of opposition before describing Gog’s defeat in detail.

f.w: I am against thee, O Gog

chapters.n: God leads Gog to the mountains of Israel—and to his ruin. The KJV’s “leave but the sixth part” is uncertain; many translations read “drive you along” or “lead you on.”

f.w: leave but the sixth part of thee
f.g: The Hebrew is obscure; it may mean “lead thee on” rather than a fraction of survivors.

chapters.n: An archer holds the bow in the left hand and arrows in the right. God knocks both away, leaving the mighty army defenseless.
Gog’s armies die on the very mountains they came to plunder, their bodies left for scavenging birds and beasts—the ultimate disgrace in the ancient world.
Gog will not even reach a city; he falls in the open countryside. God’s word guarantees the outcome.
Judgment reaches beyond the battlefield to Gog’s homeland and to distant coastlands that felt secure. “Carelessly” means in false security.

f.g: Live with a false sense of safety.
Coastlands—distant lands across the sea.

chapters.n: Through these events God’s holy name will be honored rather than mocked. He calls Himself “the Holy One in Israel,” recalling Isaiah’s favorite title.
So certain is the prophecy that God speaks of it as already finished.

f.w: it is come, and it is done

chapters.n: The enemy’s weapons become firewood—enough to burn for seven years. Seven signals completeness; the war is over for good.

f.g: Clubs or war staffs.
Seven symbolizes fullness or completion.

chapters.n: Israel won’t need to cut trees for fuel. The plunderers are plundered—a complete reversal of fortunes.

f.w: they shall spoil those that spoiled them

chapters.n: Gog receives a mass grave in a valley east of the sea (probably the Dead Sea). The valley is renamed Hamon-gog, “the multitude of Gog.” The stench blocks travelers’ way.

f.g: Hebrew “multitude (or horde) of Gog.”
“Valley of the travelers”—a route used by those passing through.

chapters.n: Burying the dead takes seven months. Under the Law of Moses, dead bodies made the land unclean, so burial is an act of purification.

f.w: that they may cleanse the land

chapters.n: The whole population joins in, and the day becomes a memorable honor for Israel because God is glorified.

f.g: Fame, honor.

chapters.n: A full-time crew is appointed to search the land and find remaining remains after the seven months.

f.g: Set apart, appoint.
Men assigned permanently to the task.

chapters.n: Anyone who sees a bone marks it so the burial crew can collect it—showing how thoroughly the land must be cleansed.
A nearby town will be named Hamonah, “multitude,” as a memorial of the event.

f.g: “Multitude”—a memorial name echoing Hamon-gog.

chapters.n: The scene shifts to grim symbolism: birds and beasts are invited to a “sacrifice” feast. In this reversal, the enemies of God become the offering.
The mighty warriors and princes are compared to fattened sacrificial animals. Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famous for its well-fed livestock.
In real sacrifice, fat and blood belonged to God alone. Here the image is reversed to show the totality of judgment on the proud.
God’s “table” is set with the horses, chariots, and warriors of a defeated army—the end of human military pride.
All nations will see God’s glory revealed in His judgments. His “hand” represents His power at work.
From that day on, Israel will know the Lord as their God. Deliverance produces lasting recognition.
Now the nations will understand that Israel’s exile was not because their God was weak, but because Israel sinned. God “hid His face”—withdrew His protection—so they fell.

f.w: hid I my face from them

chapters.n: Israel’s punishment matched their deeds. God’s justice was fair and measured.
“Now” marks the turn from judgment to mercy. God will restore Jacob’s fortunes and show compassion to the whole house of Israel.

f.w: bring again the captivity of Jacob
f.g: Restore Jacob’s fortunes; bring the captives home.

chapters.n: Once restored and safe, Israel will feel the shame of past unfaithfulness—not as condemnation, but as humble remembrance that leads to gratitude.
God’s gathering of Israel from enemy lands will display His holiness before many nations.

f.w: gathered them out of their enemies' lands

chapters.n: The same God who sent them into exile brings them all home—leaving no one behind. Both discipline and deliverance come from His hand.

f.w: have left none of them any more there

chapters.n: The section on Gog ends with a promise: God will never again hide His face, because He has poured out His Spirit on Israel. This bridges into Ezekiel’s great temple vision that follows.

f.w: I have poured out my spirit

chapters.n: Ezekiel’s final great vision (chapters 40–48) is dated to 573 BC, fourteen years after Jerusalem fell. The tenth day of the first month was the day Passover lambs were chosen—a fitting time for a vision of renewed worship.

f.w: five and twentieth year of our captivity
f.g: Counting from King Jehoiachin’s exile in 597 BC, so about 573 BC.

chapters.n: In vision Ezekiel is set on a very high mountain in Israel, where he sees something like a city. Temples are often associated with mountains in scripture—the “mountain of the Lord’s house.”

A heavenly guide gleaming like bronze stands at the gate, holding a long flax cord for large measurements and a measuring rod for smaller ones. Measuring shows that God’s house is precise, ordered, and holy.

f.w: a man, whose appearance was like the appearance of brass

chapters.n: The guide tells Ezekiel to look, listen, and pay close attention: he must report everything to Israel. The vision is meant to teach the exiles about holiness and hope.

f.w: set thine heart upon all that I shall shew thee

chapters.n: A wall surrounds the temple area. The reed is six “long cubits”—a regular cubit plus a handbreadth—about 10 to 10.5 feet (3 meters). The wall is one reed thick and one reed high.

f.w: by the cubit and an hand breadth
f.g: A “royal” or long cubit, about 20.5 inches (52 cm), instead of the common 17.5 inches.
The wall separates the holy from the common.

chapters.n: The guide begins at the east gate—the most important, since it faces the temple’s entrance and sunrise. Steps lead up to it, showing that the temple stands on higher ground.

f.w: the gate which looketh toward the east

f.g: The doorway’s floor slab.

chapters.n: Inside the gateway are small guardrooms on each side. Gate complexes like this, with chambers for guards, have been found in excavated Israelite cities.

f.g: A guardroom or alcove inside the gateway.

chapters.n: The inner vestibule of the gate is measured. The details may seem tedious, but they convey that every part of God’s house is planned with care.

f.g: A vestibule or entrance hall.

chapters.n: The vestibule and its doorposts are measured. “Posts” are thick pillars or jambs flanking the passage.

f.g: Pilasters or jambs—the side pillars of a doorway.

chapters.n: The east gate has three guardrooms on each side, all the same size—symmetry is a mark of this ideal temple.
The entrance passage is ten cubits wide and the gateway thirteen cubits long at that point.
A low barrier one cubit deep runs in front of each guardroom; the rooms are six cubits square.

f.g: A border or low barrier in front of the alcoves.

chapters.n: Measured across the gateway from the back of one guardroom to the other, it is twenty-five cubits wide.
This verse is difficult in Hebrew; it likely describes the gate’s pillars and the court around them. Translators differ on the number sixty.

f.g: Sixty cubits; the Hebrew here is obscure, and translations vary.

chapters.n: From front to back, the whole gate complex is fifty cubits long—about 85 feet.
The gate has narrow windows and is decorated with palm trees, as Solomon’s temple was. Palms suggest life, fruitfulness, and the garden of Eden.

f.g: Possibly recessed or latticed openings.

chapters.n: Ezekiel enters the outer court, which has a paved area with thirty rooms along it—likely used by worshippers for meals and gatherings.

f.g: The outer courtyard where ordinary Israelites worshipped.

chapters.n: The lower pavement runs alongside the gates. The inner court is higher, so worshippers climb as they approach holiness.
The distance from the outer gate to the inner gate is a hundred cubits on the east and on the north.
Now the north gate of the outer court is measured. It mirrors the east gate exactly.
Same guardrooms, same pillars, same dimensions: fifty by twenty-five cubits. Repetition emphasizes perfect order.
Seven steps lead up to the outer gates. Seven often suggests completeness in scripture.

f.g: The outer gates rise by seven steps; the inner gates by eight (verses 31, 34, 37).

chapters.n: Each outer gate lines up with an inner gate, a hundred cubits apart. The plan is balanced on every side.

f.g: Opposite, facing.

chapters.n: The guide moves to the south gate of the outer court, which also matches the others.
The south gate has the same windows and dimensions—fifty by twenty-five cubits.
Seven steps and palm decorations on the doorposts, just like the other outer gates.
Opposite the outer south gate stands an inner gate, again a hundred cubits away.
Ezekiel is brought into the inner court through its south gate, which has the same measurements as the outer gates.

f.g: The court closer to the sanctuary, reserved for priests in Ezekiel’s plan.

chapters.n: The inner south gate has guardrooms, pillars, and windows like the outer ones—fifty by twenty-five cubits.
This verse, missing from some ancient manuscripts, gives measurements for the vestibules (arches) around the gate.

f.g: Hebrew ʾelammim—probably vestibules or porches, not curved arches.

chapters.n: The inner gates face outward toward the outer court and are reached by eight steps—one more than the outer gates. Each step brings the worshipper higher, symbolically closer to God.

f.g: The inner court stands higher than the outer court.
Outer court (“utter” = outer).

chapters.n: Next, the inner east gate is measured—the gate in line with the temple’s entrance.
Its dimensions match the others, fifty by twenty-five cubits.
Like the other inner gates, it has palm decorations and eight steps.
Finally the inner north gate is measured, completing the circuit of the gates.
All its parts match the standard—guardrooms, pillars, vestibules, windows, fifty by twenty-five cubits.
Palm trees and eight steps again. The repetition across six gates stresses that the whole temple is harmonious and consistent.
Near the inner gates is a room for washing burnt offerings. Cleanliness was required for anything placed on God’s altar.
Tables in the gate vestibule are for slaughtering three kinds of sacrifice: burnt offerings (complete devotion), sin offerings, and trespass offerings (for guilt).
More tables stand outside the north gate. The north side of the altar was the traditional place for slaughtering burnt offerings.
Eight tables in all are used for slaughtering sacrifices—a well-organized area for priestly service.
Four cut-stone tables, small and low, hold the knives and tools used in the sacrifices.

f.g: Dressed or cut stone.

chapters.n: Hooks or ledges a handbreadth wide line the room for hanging or resting the meat of the offerings.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean double hooks or ledges.

chapters.n: Rooms for singers stand in the inner court. Music had been part of temple worship since David organized the Levite choirs.

f.g: Facing direction, outlook.

chapters.n: One of these rooms belongs to priests responsible for the temple building itself.

f.w: keepers of the charge of the house
f.g: Priests on duty for the care of the temple.

chapters.n: The other room is for priests who serve at the altar—the descendants of Zadok, who stayed faithful when other priests strayed. Zadok was high priest in Solomon’s day.
The inner court is a perfect square, a hundred cubits each way, with the altar standing in front of the temple. Squares signify perfection and order.

f.g: Perfectly square.

chapters.n: Ezekiel is brought to the porch of the temple itself. The doorposts and entrance are measured.
The porch is twenty by eleven (or twelve) cubits, reached by steps and flanked by two pillars—echoing Solomon’s bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz.
The guide moves from the porch into the temple building itself. The entrance pillars are six cubits thick—massive, as befits the house of God.

f.g: Here simply “tent” or dwelling—an echo of the wilderness tabernacle where God dwelt among Israel.

chapters.n: The main hall, the Holy Place, is forty by twenty cubits—exactly the size of the Holy Place in Solomon’s temple.

f.w: forty cubits: and the breadth, twenty cubits

chapters.n: Only the guide goes further inward; Ezekiel, though a priest, stays back. The entrances narrow as one approaches the holiest room—a picture of increasing sacredness.

f.g: Ezekiel does not enter the most holy place himself.

chapters.n: The Most Holy Place is a perfect cube in floor plan, twenty by twenty cubits, as in Solomon’s temple. Here God’s presence dwelt; in ancient Israel only the high priest entered, once a year.

f.w: This is the most holy place

chapters.n: The temple’s walls are six cubits thick, and along the outside are side rooms four cubits wide—likely storerooms for temple supplies.

f.g: Storage rooms built against the outer walls.

chapters.n: The side rooms rise three stories, thirty to a level. Their beams rest on ledges rather than being cut into the temple wall, so the sanctuary wall is not pierced.

f.w: they had not hold in the wall of the house

chapters.n: The side rooms get wider on each higher floor because the temple wall steps inward. A stairway or ramp leads up through the levels.

f.g: A stairway or ramp leading upward.

chapters.n: The temple stands on a raised platform six long cubits high—lifting the sanctuary above its surroundings.

f.w: a full reed of six great cubits
f.g: About 10 feet (3 meters).

chapters.n: The outer wall of the side rooms is five cubits thick, with an open terrace beyond it.
A twenty-cubit open space surrounds the temple, separating it from the priests’ buildings.
Doors from the side rooms open north and south onto the terrace, which is five cubits wide.

f.g: An open, unbuilt area or terrace.

chapters.n: Behind the temple on the west stands a large separate building, seventy by ninety cubits. Its purpose isn’t stated; it may have been for storage or service.

f.g: A restricted or set-apart yard behind the temple.

chapters.n: The temple and its surroundings measure a hundred cubits long—another perfect, round number showing completeness.
The east front of the temple with its adjoining yard is also a hundred cubits wide, so the temple area is a perfect square.
The western building and its galleries are a hundred cubits as well. Everything fits a symmetrical, harmonious plan.

f.g: Possibly terraces or colonnades; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

chapters.n: The interior is paneled with wood from floor to windows, with framed windows and three levels of galleries.

f.g: Paneled or lined with wood.

chapters.n: The walls inside and out, even above the doors, are all decorated according to careful measure.
Carvings alternate cherubim and palm trees. In Solomon’s temple the same designs recalled Eden, where cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life.

f.g: Unlike the four-faced cherubim of Ezekiel 1, these show two faces in the flat carving.

chapters.n: Each cherub has the face of a man turned toward one palm and the face of a lion toward another, repeated all around the house.
The cherubim and palms cover the walls from floor to above the doors.
The doorposts are square, and the entrance to the sanctuary matches the outer one—consistency throughout.
A wooden altar stands before the Most Holy Place. The guide calls it “the table that is before the LORD,” likely corresponding to the table of shewbread or the incense altar.

f.w: This is the table that is before the LORD

chapters.n: Both the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place have doors.
Each door has two folding leaves that turn on hinges, like Solomon’s temple doors.
The doors bear the same cherubim and palm carvings as the walls. A wooden canopy or threshold covers the outside of the porch.

f.g: Possibly a wooden canopy or overhang; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: The porch walls and side rooms have narrow windows and palm decorations. The whole building is beautiful and orderly—fitting for the place God would dwell.
The guide leads Ezekiel into the outer court on the north side to see a building of priestly chambers beside the restricted yard behind the temple.

f.g: Outer court.

chapters.n: The chamber building is a hundred cubits long and fifty wide, with its entrance on the north.
The chambers face both the inner court’s open space and the outer court’s pavement, rising in three terraced stories.

f.g: Terraces or balconies stepped back level by level.

chapters.n: A ten-cubit walkway runs along the chambers. The phrase “a way of one cubit” may be a copyist’s slip for “a hundred cubits.”
Because each story is set back, the upper rooms are narrower than the lower ones.
Without supporting pillars like those of the courts, the upper floors had to be stepped back, making them smaller.

f.g: Narrowed, made smaller.

chapters.n: A fifty-cubit outer wall screens the chambers from the outer court, giving privacy to the priests.
The chambers toward the outer court are fifty cubits long, while those facing the temple run a hundred cubits.
An entrance on the east side lets people reach the chambers from the outer court.
A matching set of chambers stands on the south side. The temple complex is symmetrical in every direction.

f.g: Many ancient versions read “toward the south,” fitting the context.

chapters.n: The south chambers mirror the north chambers in size, layout, exits, and doors.
An entrance at the head of the passage leads into the south chambers as well.
The chambers’ purpose: here the priests eat their holy portions of the offerings and store the most holy things. Holiness requires designated, set-apart space.

f.g: Grain offering; “meat” in KJV English meant food in general.

chapters.n: Priests must change out of their sacred clothing before going out among the people. Their garments are holy and must not be mixed with common life—a lesson in reverence for sacred things.

f.w: there they shall lay their garments wherein they minister

chapters.n: With the inner temple measured, the guide leads Ezekiel out the east gate to measure the entire complex.
The east side measures five hundred units. The Hebrew says “reeds,” but many think “cubits” was intended (about 850 feet); the Greek Old Testament reads cubits.

f.g: Possibly 500 cubits; if reeds, the area would be about a mile square.

chapters.n: The north side measures the same.
The south side matches.
The west side completes the square.
The whole temple area is a perfect square surrounded by a wall to separate the holy from the common. The lesson: God’s presence calls for clear boundaries between the sacred and the profane.

f.w: to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place

f.g: Common, ordinary—not necessarily evil, but not set apart as holy.

chapters.n: Ezekiel is brought back to the east gate—the very gate through which he had seen God’s glory leave the temple years before.

f.w: the gate that looketh toward the east

chapters.n: This is the climax of the whole book: the glory of God returns from the east. His voice roars like a great waterfall, and the land shines with His light.

f.w: his voice was like a noise of many waters
the earth shined with his glory

chapters.n: Ezekiel recognizes the same vision he saw by the river Chebar and when God departed from Jerusalem. Overwhelmed, he falls on his face in reverence.

f.w: when I came to destroy the city
f.g: When Ezekiel came in vision to announce the city’s destruction.

chapters.n: The glory enters the temple by the east gate. What departed in chapters 10–11 now returns—God is coming home to His people.

f.w: the glory of the LORD came into the house

chapters.n: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel into the inner court, and he sees the glory of the Lord filling the house, as it once filled the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple.

f.w: the glory of the LORD filled the house

chapters.n: The Lord speaks from inside the temple while the guide stands beside Ezekiel.
God calls the temple His throne and footstool, where He will live among Israel forever. Israel must never again defile it with idolatry or with royal monuments placed near His house.

f.g: Spiritual unfaithfulness—worshipping other gods.
Possibly royal tombs or memorial monuments to dead kings, or to idols called “kings.”

chapters.n: In Solomon’s day the royal palace was built right next to the temple, separated only by a wall. The kings’ sins happened, as it were, on God’s doorstep.
God’s promise is conditional and generous: if Israel removes its idolatry, He will dwell with them forever.

f.w: I will dwell in the midst of them for ever

chapters.n: Ezekiel is to describe the temple so Israel will feel ashamed of their sins. Seeing God’s holiness helps people recognize their need to change.

f.w: that they may be ashamed of their iniquities

f.g: Plan or design; Hebrew toknit, a measured layout.

chapters.n: If they repent, Ezekiel should show them all the details—the design, entrances, exits, laws, and ordinances—and write them down so Israel can follow them.
The central principle—“the law of the house”—is that the whole mountaintop area surrounding the temple is most holy. Holiness extends outward from God’s presence.

f.w: This is the law of the house
f.g: The governing rule of the temple: everything within its bounds is sacred.

f.w: Upon the top of the mountain

chapters.n: Now the altar of burnt offering is described. Its base includes a gutter one cubit deep with a rim a span high, probably to collect blood from the sacrifices.

f.g: About half a cubit—the distance across a spread hand, roughly 9 inches.

chapters.n: The altar rises in stepped levels called “settles”—ledges that narrow toward the top, somewhat like a small ziggurat.

f.g: A ledge or stepped platform.

chapters.n: The top hearth is four cubits high, with four horns rising from the corners. The horns were the most sacred part of the altar, where blood was applied.

f.g: Hebrew harʾel—“mountain of God” or “altar hearth.”

chapters.n: The altar’s hearth is twelve cubits square—echoing the twelve tribes of Israel.
The ledge below is fourteen cubits square. Steps face east, so the priest climbing them faces west toward the temple—turning his back on the rising sun, which pagans worshipped.

f.w: his stairs shall look toward the east

chapters.n: The Lord gives instructions for dedicating the altar—how it is to be prepared before sacrifices can be offered.
A young bull is given to the Zadokite priests for a sin offering. In this vision Ezekiel himself oversees the dedication, much as Moses did for the tabernacle.

f.w: a young bullock for a sin offering

chapters.n: Blood is applied to the horns, corners, and rim to purify the altar. In the Law of Moses, blood represented life and was the means of atonement—pointing ahead to Christ’s atoning blood.
The bull’s body is burned outside the sanctuary. Hebrews draws on this practice to describe Jesus suffering “without the gate.”
On the second day, an unblemished male goat is offered as a sin offering, cleansing the altar again.

f.g: Free of physical defects—required for sacrifices, pointing to Christ’s sinlessness.

chapters.n: After the cleansing comes a burnt offering of a young bull and a ram—a gift wholly given to God.
The priests sprinkle salt on the offerings. Salt symbolized preservation and lasting covenant.
The dedication lasts seven days, with daily offerings—like the seven-day consecration of Aaron and his sons.
For seven days the altar is purified, and the priests are consecrated—literally their “hands are filled,” a Hebrew idiom for installing priests.

f.g: Hebrew “fill its hand”—an idiom for ordaining or dedicating.

chapters.n: From the eighth day onward, regular worship begins and God promises, “I will accept you.” Acceptance by God is the goal of all temple worship.

f.g: Fellowship offerings, partly eaten by the worshippers in a sacred meal.

chapters.n: Ezekiel is brought back to the outer east gate and finds it closed.
The gate stays shut because the Lord Himself entered through it. A path made holy by God’s presence is not used for ordinary traffic—and the closed gate also signals that God will never leave again.

f.w: the LORD, the God of Israel, hath entered in by it

chapters.n: Only “the prince”—Israel’s ruler in this vision—may sit in the gateway to eat a sacred meal before the Lord, entering and leaving through its vestibule.

f.g: The leader of restored Israel in Ezekiel’s vision; notably called “prince,” not “king.”

f.w: to eat bread before the LORD

chapters.n: At the north gate Ezekiel again sees God’s glory filling the temple, and again falls on his face. Each encounter renews his awe.
The Lord tells Ezekiel to pay close attention to all the temple’s rules, especially who may come in and go out. Access to holy places is the theme of this chapter.

f.g: Literally “set your heart”—pay careful attention.

chapters.n: God addresses Israel as “the rebellious” and says, in effect, “Enough of your abominations!”

f.g: “Enough!”—stop now.

chapters.n: One sin was letting unconsecrated foreigners—people with no covenant commitment—serve in the sanctuary. Being uncircumcised in heart means lacking inner devotion to God.

f.w: my bread, the fat and the blood
f.g: The parts of offerings belonging to God.

chapters.n: Instead of guarding God’s holy things themselves, Israel had handed temple duties to others for convenience.

f.g: Duty, responsibility, assigned watch.

chapters.n: No one who lacks covenant commitment, inside or out, may enter the sanctuary. Worthiness for holy places is required.
The Levites who led or followed Israel into idolatry will bear the consequences of their sin.

f.w: the Levites that are gone away far from me

chapters.n: Still, they are not cast out; they may serve as gatekeepers and helpers, slaughtering sacrifices for the people. God’s discipline is real, but He still gives them a place.
They had served people at idol shrines and led Israel astray. God raised His hand in oath against them—they must accept the consequences.
These Levites may not act as priests or handle the most holy things. Loss of privilege is the consequence of past unfaithfulness.
They will be put in charge of the temple’s practical needs—a humbler but still meaningful service.
The sons of Zadok, who stayed faithful when others strayed, may come near to God and offer sacrifices. Faithfulness in hard times brings greater trust.
These priests may enter the sanctuary and approach God’s table, serving in His presence.
Priests serving in the inner court must wear linen, not wool. Linen symbolized purity, and in heaven too the righteous are pictured in fine linen.
Linen turbans and undergarments are required, avoiding anything that makes them sweat—sweat recalls the curse of toil after the Fall and was considered unfit for holy service.

f.g: Turbans or headdresses.
Undergarments covering the loins.

chapters.n: Before going out among the people, priests change out of their sacred clothing and leave it in the holy chambers. Holy things are kept separate from common use.

f.w: they shall not sanctify the people with their garments
f.g: Contact with holy garments was thought to pass holiness on, creating ritual complications.

chapters.n: Priests must neither shave their heads (a mourning or pagan custom) nor grow their hair wild. They are to keep it neatly trimmed.

f.g: Trim the hair.

f.w: Neither shall they shave their heads

chapters.n: No priest may drink wine before serving in the inner court. Sacred service requires a clear mind.

f.w: Neither shall any priest drink wine

chapters.n: Priests must marry virgins of Israel or widows of other priests. This guarded the priestly family line and its holiness.

f.g: A divorced woman.

f.w: Neither shall they take for their wives a widow

chapters.n: A key duty of priests: teaching people to tell the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean. Spiritual discernment is learned.

f.w: the difference between the holy and profane

chapters.n: Priests also act as judges in disputes, rule by God’s law, and keep the Sabbaths holy.

f.w: in controversy they shall stand in judgment

chapters.n: Contact with a corpse caused ritual impurity. Priests may only become unclean for their closest relatives.

f.w: they shall come at no dead person

chapters.n: After being purified from contact with the dead, a priest waits another seven days before serving.
On returning to service, he must offer a sin offering—a reminder that even priests need atonement.

f.w: he shall offer his sin offering

chapters.n: Priests receive no land. God Himself is their inheritance—a beautiful idea: those devoted to God’s service find their true wealth in Him.
Instead of land, priests live from portions of the offerings and anything dedicated to God.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem—items devoted entirely to God.

chapters.n: The first and best of everything goes to the priests, including the first of the bread dough. Giving the first portion brings God’s blessing to the household.

f.g: An offering or contribution.

chapters.n: Priests must not eat animals that died naturally or were killed by beasts—such meat was unclean.
When the land is divided, a holy strip is first set apart for the Lord—25,000 by 10,000 units (likely cubits, about 8 by 3 miles). God receives the first portion before the tribes receive theirs.

f.g: An offering or contribution—here a gift of land set apart for God.

chapters.n: Within it, the temple occupies a 500-by-500 square with a 50-cubit open buffer around it to protect its holiness.

f.g: Open land or pasture around a site—here a buffer zone.

chapters.n: In this holy portion will stand the sanctuary and the most holy place. The temple is literally at the center of Israel’s life.
The priests’ homes are built in this holy area, near the sanctuary they serve.

f.w: the priests the ministers of the sanctuary

chapters.n: An equal strip is given to the Levites for their homes and towns. The Greek Old Testament reads “cities to dwell in” instead of “twenty chambers.”

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; some ancient versions read “towns to live in.”

chapters.n: Beside the holy portion lies a strip for the city, belonging to all Israel—not to one tribe. Jerusalem becomes a shared possession.

f.w: it shall be for the whole house of Israel

chapters.n: The prince receives land on both sides of the holy area, stretching east and west. His property is defined and limited.

f.w: a portion shall be for the prince

chapters.n: Because the prince has his own land, he will no longer seize land from the people. Past kings like Ahab had taken what wasn’t theirs.

f.w: my princes shall no more oppress my people

chapters.n: A direct charge to Israel’s rulers: stop violence and robbery, do what is just and right, and end unfair taxation of the people.

f.g: Forced payments, evictions, or seizures.

chapters.n: Honest weights and measures are required. Cheating with false scales was a common way the powerful exploited the poor.

f.g: A dry measure for grain, about two-thirds of a bushel.
A liquid measure, roughly 6 gallons (22 liters).

chapters.n: The ephah (dry) and bath (liquid) are made equal, each one-tenth of a homer—standardizing the system so no one can cheat.

f.g: A large measure, originally a donkey-load—about 6 bushels.

chapters.n: Money weights are standardized too: twenty gerahs make a shekel, and sixty shekels make a maneh (mina).

f.g: The smallest unit of weight, about half a gram.
Mina—a larger weight; here 20 + 25 + 15 = 60 shekels.

chapters.n: The people’s contribution is set: one-sixtieth of their wheat and barley harvest.
Of olive oil, one percent is given—a tenth of a bath from every cor (ten baths).

f.g: A large measure equal to a homer.

chapters.n: One lamb from every two hundred is given for offerings that “make reconciliation”—atonement that restores the relationship between God and His people.

f.g: Hebrew kipper—to atone, cover, or reconcile.

chapters.n: The whole population brings these gifts to the prince, who will provide the national offerings.
The prince is responsible for providing offerings at all the festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths. Leadership here is service to the community’s worship.

f.g: The first day of each month, marked with offerings.
Wine poured out as an offering.

chapters.n: On New Year’s Day, the first day of the first month (spring), a young bull is sacrificed to purify the sanctuary.
The blood is applied to the doorposts of the temple, the altar’s ledge, and the inner gate—like Passover blood on doorposts.

f.w: upon the posts of the house

chapters.n: The cleansing is repeated on the seventh day for anyone who sinned by mistake or out of ignorance. God provides for unintentional sins.

f.g: Naive, inexperienced, or ignorant.

chapters.n: Passover is kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, followed by a week of unleavened bread—remembering deliverance from Egypt.
On Passover day the prince provides a sin offering for himself and all the people. Even the ruler needs atonement.
Every day of the feast, seven bulls and seven rams are offered, plus a goat for sin—a lavish, complete offering.

f.g: Seven represents completeness; the amounts differ from Numbers 28:16-25.

chapters.n: Grain offerings and oil accompany the animal sacrifices. A hin was about a gallon.

f.g: A liquid measure, roughly a gallon (3.7 liters).

chapters.n: The same pattern is followed for the autumn festival on the fifteenth day of the seventh month—the Feast of Tabernacles.

f.w: the feast of the seven days
f.g: The Feast of Tabernacles (Booths).

chapters.n: The inner east gate stays closed on the six working days but opens on the Sabbath and the new moon. Holy time and holy space work together: special days bring special access.

f.w: on the sabbath it shall be opened

chapters.n: The prince stands at the gate’s threshold while priests offer his sacrifices. He worships but does not go into the priests’ inner court—even a ruler has limits before God.

f.w: he shall worship at the threshold of the gate
f.g: The prince bows in worship at the doorway rather than entering the priests’ court.

chapters.n: The common people also worship at the entrance to this gate on Sabbaths and new moons, sharing in the view toward God’s house.

f.g: The general population of Israel.

chapters.n: The prince’s Sabbath offering is six lambs and a ram—larger than the Sabbath offering in the Law of Moses.
Grain offerings accompany the animals: an ephah for the ram and whatever the prince can afford for the lambs, with oil.

f.w: as he shall be able to give
f.g: Literally “the gift of his hand”—as much as he wishes.

chapters.n: On the new moon, a young bull is added to the lambs and ram—marking the start of each month with worship.
The grain offering is matched to each animal, with flexibility for the lambs according to what he can give.

f.w: according as his hand shall attain unto
f.g: As much as he is able.

chapters.n: The prince enters and leaves through the same gate vestibule.
At the great festivals, worshippers who come in by the north gate leave by the south, and vice versa. This keeps crowds flowing—and symbolically, no one leaves God’s presence the same way they came.

f.w: he shall not return by the way of the gate whereby he came in
f.g: Many readers see a lesson here: worship should change the worshipper’s direction.

chapters.n: On festival days the prince worships among the people, going in and out with them—a leader who stands with his people, not above them.
Grain offerings at feasts follow the same measures given for the Sabbath and new moon.

f.g: Appointed holy festivals.

chapters.n: For freewill offerings—gifts given beyond what is required—the east gate is opened for the prince and then shut after he leaves.

f.g: A freewill offering, given from gratitude, not obligation.

chapters.n: Every morning a year-old lamb is offered as a burnt offering—daily devotion at the start of each day.
Fine flour and oil accompany the morning lamb as a perpetual ordinance.

f.g: Moisten, mix.
A lasting rule.

chapters.n: This continual offering is a constant reminder of Israel’s covenant with God, renewed each day.

f.g: Hebrew tamid—“continual,” the daily offering.

chapters.n: If the prince gives land to one of his sons, it becomes the son’s permanent inheritance.
If he gives land to a servant, it returns to the prince in the year of liberty. Royal land stays in the family and cannot be used to build a power network.

f.g: The Jubilee year, every fiftieth year, when land returned to its original owners.

chapters.n: The prince may not seize the people’s land to enrich his family. This guards ordinary Israelites from royal greed and keeps families on their inherited land.

f.w: the prince shall not take of the people's inheritance

chapters.n: Ezekiel is led to the priests’ chambers on the north side and shown a place at the far west end.
Here priests cook the guilt and sin offerings and bake the grain offerings, so holy food is not carried into the outer court where people might contact it.

f.g: Contact with most holy things would bring people under special ritual restrictions.

chapters.n: Back in the outer court, Ezekiel sees a small court in each of its four corners.
The four corner courts are equal in size, forty by thirty cubits.

f.g: Possibly “enclosed” or “small” courts; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: Each corner court has a low wall with hearths built beneath it for cooking.

f.g: Cooking hearths.

chapters.n: These are kitchens where the Levites cook the people’s sacrifices for sacred meals. Worship included joyful communal meals in God’s presence.

f.g: Peace offerings eaten by worshippers and their families.

chapters.n: One of the most beautiful images in scripture: water flows out from under the temple’s threshold, eastward past the altar. Life-giving blessing springs from the place of God’s presence. Joseph Smith taught that this prophecy would be fulfilled in the last days with a temple in Jerusalem.

f.w: waters issued out from under the threshold of the house

chapters.n: The east gate is shut, so the guide leads Ezekiel out the north gate and around to see the stream trickling out on the south side of the east gate.

f.g: Hebrew suggests a trickle, as if from a small flask—the stream starts tiny.

chapters.n: About a third of a mile downstream, the water is ankle-deep. Ezekiel wades through it himself.

f.g: About 1,700 feet (520 meters).

chapters.n: Every thousand cubits the water rises—knee-deep, then waist-deep—with no tributaries feeding it. God’s blessing grows in ways nature cannot explain.

f.g: The waist and hips.

chapters.n: Finally it becomes a river too deep to cross—water to swim in. What began as a trickle becomes overwhelming abundance.
“Have you seen this?” The guide wants Ezekiel to grasp the meaning, then leads him back to the riverbank.
Ezekiel now notices many trees lining both banks—an oasis in what was once desert.
The river flows east through the barren Judean wilderness down to the Dead Sea, whose salty water will be made fresh. A dead sea comes to life.

f.g: The Dead Sea, so salty that almost nothing lives in it.

chapters.n: Wherever the river goes, life follows—swarms of creatures and abundant fish. It is a picture of how God’s presence brings life to everything it touches.

f.w: every thing shall live whither the river cometh

chapters.n: Fishermen will line the shore from En-gedi to En-eglaim, drying their nets, with as many kinds of fish as the Mediterranean. En-gedi is an oasis on the Dead Sea’s western shore.

f.g: A spring and oasis on the west shore of the Dead Sea.
The Mediterranean Sea.

chapters.n: Some marshes will stay salty—useful as a source of salt, an important resource. Not everything changes, but what remains has purpose.

f.g: Swamps, muddy areas.

chapters.n: Fruit trees on both banks never wither and bear fresh fruit every month. Their fruit nourishes and their leaves heal—because their water comes from the sanctuary. Revelation picks up this image for the tree of life.

f.g: For food.

f.w: because their waters they issued out of the sanctuary

chapters.n: Now God sets the boundaries of the land for the twelve tribes. Joseph gets two portions—one for each of his sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as Jacob had promised.
The land is divided equally among the tribes, fulfilling God’s oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

f.g: Equally, each the same.

f.w: I lifted up mine hand to give it unto your fathers

chapters.n: The northern border runs from the Mediterranean inland toward Hethlon and Zedad, in the region of modern Lebanon and Syria.

f.g: The Mediterranean.

chapters.n: More northern landmarks are listed, around Hamath and Damascus. These match the ideal borders described in Moses’ day.

f.g: A city on the Orontes River in Syria, marking Israel’s ideal northern limit.

chapters.n: The northern line ends at Hazar-enan, near the border of Damascus.
The eastern border is the Jordan River down to the Dead Sea. Notably, the land east of the Jordan (Gilead) is not included.

f.g: The Dead Sea.

chapters.n: The southern border runs from Tamar to the springs of Kadesh, then along the Brook of Egypt to the Mediterranean.

f.w: the waters of strife in Kadesh
f.g: Meribah-Kadesh, where Israel quarreled with Moses over water.
The Wadi of Egypt, a seasonal stream in the northern Sinai.

chapters.n: The western border is the Mediterranean coast.
The land is to be divided among the tribes of Israel according to these borders.
A remarkable provision: foreigners who live among Israel and raise families there receive an inheritance just like native-born Israelites. God’s people include those who join them.

f.w: to the strangers that sojourn among you

chapters.n: The stranger receives land within whatever tribe he lives among—fully integrated into the covenant people.

f.g: Lives as a resident foreigner.

chapters.n: The land is divided into horizontal strips running east to west, one for each tribe. Dan, which had migrated to the far north in the time of the judges, receives the northernmost strip.
Asher, a son of Jacob through Zilpah (Leah’s handmaid), receives the next strip south.
Naphtali, son of Bilhah (Rachel’s handmaid), comes next. The tribes descended from the handmaids are placed farthest from the sanctuary.
Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn, receives a strip—part of Joseph’s double portion.
Ephraim, Joseph’s younger son who received the greater blessing, receives the strip next to Manasseh. Together they form Joseph’s two shares.
Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, is placed here. He lost his birthright through sin, yet still receives an equal portion.
Judah, the royal tribe, borders the holy portion on the north. Unlike in Joshua’s day, Judah is now north of Jerusalem.
Between Judah and Benjamin lies the special strip offered to God, with the sanctuary at its heart.

f.w: the sanctuary shall be in the midst of it

chapters.n: The section set apart for the Lord is 25,000 by 10,000—the priests’ portion with the temple.
The priests’ section is described on all four sides, with the Lord’s sanctuary at the center. God is literally central to Israel’s life.
This land belongs to the faithful Zadokite priests, who did not go astray when Israel and many Levites did.
This is a “most holy” portion, lying next to the Levites’ land.
The Levites receive an equal-sized strip adjacent to the priests.
This land may not be sold, traded, or transferred. As the “firstfruits” of the land, it belongs to the Lord permanently.

f.g: Transfer ownership to someone else.

chapters.n: The remaining 5,000-wide strip is ordinary land for the city, its homes, and open fields. The city is set apart from, but beside, the holy area.

f.g: Common, not consecrated—not “unholy” in the sense of sinful.

chapters.n: The city is a perfect square, 4,500 units on each side—like the temple, a symbol of order and wholeness.
A 250-unit open belt surrounds the city on every side.

f.g: Open pasture land around the city.

chapters.n: Farmland on either side of the city produces food for the city’s workers.

f.g: Its produce or harvest.

chapters.n: Workers for the city come from every tribe of Israel. The capital belongs to the whole nation, not to one tribe.
The entire sacred area—priests, Levites, and city—forms a 25,000-by-25,000 square.

f.g: A perfect square.

chapters.n: Land east and west of the sacred square belongs to the prince, giving him a defined estate so he won’t oppress the people.

f.w: the residue shall be for the prince

chapters.n: The prince’s land lies between the borders of Judah and Benjamin, flanking the holy portion.
South of the holy area, Benjamin receives the first strip. Judah and Benjamin—the two tribes of the old southern kingdom—frame the sanctuary.
Simeon, whose territory was once absorbed into Judah, now has its own strip.
Issachar, once in the north near the Jezreel Valley, is relocated south in this vision.
Zebulun likewise receives a southern portion.
Gad, once east of the Jordan, now receives land west of it in the far south.
Gad’s southern boundary is the southern border of the whole land, from Tamar to Kadesh and the Brook of Egypt.

f.w: the waters of strife in Kadesh

chapters.n: This completes the division. Every tribe is restored and every tribe has a place—a picture of a fully gathered Israel.

f.w: divide by lot unto the tribes of Israel

chapters.n: The city’s exits are now described, beginning with the north side, 4,500 units long.

f.g: Exits or gates.

chapters.n: The city has twelve gates named for the tribes. On the north: Reuben, Judah, and Levi. Revelation’s New Jerusalem also has twelve gates bearing the tribes’ names.

f.w: the gates of the city shall be after the names of the tribes of Israel

chapters.n: On the east: Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan. Here Joseph and Levi are both included, so Ephraim and Manasseh share one gate as “Joseph.”
On the south: Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun.
On the west: Gad, Asher, and Naphtali. All twelve sons of Jacob have a gate—every tribe has access to the holy city.

Ezekiel ends with the city’s new name: “The LORD is there” (Hebrew Yahweh Shammah). The book that began with God’s glory leaving Jerusalem closes with His permanent presence among His people—the ultimate hope of the gospel.

f.g: Hebrew Yahweh Shammah.
The city’s circumference: four sides of 4,500.
